title: Genetics
tagline: What a gene actually is, how variation works, and the parts that change decisions: what a polygenic score can and cannot tell you, how to read a positive test, which genes already change prescribing, and what gene editing can do today.
description: From the molecule up to the clinic. The molecular half is the foundation — genes, transcription, the variation inventory, Mendelian patterns and the penetrance that breaks them. The quantitative half is where most public understanding goes wrong: heritability is a population variance ratio, not a verdict on an individual; a GWAS hit is an association with an odds ratio near 1.1, not a 'gene for' anything; and a polygenic score places you on a curve rather than diagnosing you. The clinical half is what is actionable now: pharmacogenomics that already changes prescribing, the germline/somatic split in cancer, and the gene-editing therapies that reached approval.

intro.hook: Three billion letters, written in a four-letter alphabet, copied into every cell you have.
body: The instructions for building and running you are a chemical text. Not a metaphor — an actual sequence of four molecules whose order carries meaning, copied with astonishing fidelity every time a cell divides, and passed to your children with a few thousand changes.

In one lifetime this went from unknown to routine. The structure was solved in 1953. The first human genome took thirteen years and roughly three billion dollars. It now costs a few hundred and takes a day.

This course covers what the text says, how it is read, how it varies between people, and what we can and cannot currently conclude from it — including the parts where public understanding has run considerably ahead of the science.

why.title: It is personal
why.text: Drug response, disease risk and inherited traits are increasingly read directly from sequence — including yours.

why.title: One mechanism, enormous reach
why.text: Copy, read, translate, regulate. Every organism on Earth uses the same scheme with the same alphabet.

why.title: Where the claims outrun the data
why.text: Heritability, polygenic scores and "a gene for X" are widely misreported. Knowing the limits is half the literacy.

intro.closer: Every cell carries the whole text. What makes a neuron a neuron is which parts it reads.

concepts.title: What Is a Gene? — 3.1 billion letters, ~19,400 genes
concepts.summary: The human genome is enormous, the protein-coding parts list is startlingly small, and the fight over what the rest does is not as settled as either side claims.

cards.h: 3.1 billion letters, packed into 46 chromosomes
cards.md:
Your genome is **~3.1 billion base pairs** (**Gb**, gigabases) per haploid set — the 23 chromosomes you inherited from one parent. You carry two sets, so ~6.2 Gb per nucleus, roughly **2 metres** of DNA if stretched end to end.

The reference genome was declared 'complete' in 2003 at about **92% coverage**. The missing ~8% was not random: centromeres, ribosomal DNA arrays and segmental duplications — highly repetitive sequence that short reads cannot be placed into uniquely. Those gaps were closed in 2022 by the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium: **T2T-CHM13 is 3.055 Gb with no gaps** (Nurk et al., *Science* 2022), adding ~200 **Mb** (megabases) of sequence nobody had ever read.

Scale is uneven — chromosome 1 is ~248 Mb, chromosome 21 only ~47 Mb.

And 'the' human genome is a convenient fiction. The current standard is a **pangenome**: a graph of many independent assemblies, because a single linear reference systematically under-represents variation in the populations it was not built from.

cards.h: Only ~19,400 protein-coding genes — and why that was a shock
cards.md:
Before the Human Genome Project reported, the informal betting pool on gene count ran from **50,000 to 140,000**. The answer came in far lower and has only tightened since.

**GENCODE release 50** — the reference annotation behind Ensembl and most clinical pipelines — lists:

- **19,442 protein-coding genes**
- **35,885 long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes** — transcribed, never translated into protein
- **644,292 transcripts** in total

Protein-coding **exon** (the retained, translated stretches) accounts for roughly **1.5% of the genome**.

And ~19,400 is not a large number. *Caenorhabditis elegans*, a 1-mm nematode built from 959 cells, carries about 20,000. Rice has more genes than you do.

**That is the organising fact for this whole pack.** If complexity does not live in the parts count, it lives in (a) how parts are **combined** — alternative splicing turns 19,442 coding genes into hundreds of thousands of distinct transcripts — and (b) **when and where** each is switched on. What distinguishes a neuron from a liver cell is overwhelmingly **regulatory** information, not coding information.

cards.h: 'Junk DNA' and what ENCODE actually established
cards.md:
Susumu Ohno coined **'junk DNA'** in 1972 for the non-coding ~98.5%. About half the genome is **transposable elements** — mobile repeats, the vast majority long dead — which made the label plausible.

As a blanket claim it was wrong. Non-coding sequence holds promoters, enhancers, insulators, lncRNAs, microRNAs and structural elements, and **most disease associations found by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) fall in non-coding DNA**, not in genes.

But the correction over-shot. **ENCODE** (Encyclopedia of DNA Elements) announced in 2012 that **'80% of the genome is biochemically functional.'** That headline conflated *biochemical activity* — transcribed once, or bound by one protein, in one cell type — with *function*, meaning maintained by natural selection. Graur and colleagues (2013) and Doolittle (2013) attacked it hard and the criticism largely stuck. Comparative-genomics estimates of the fraction under **purifying selection** sit near **5–8%**, not 80%.

**What ENCODE did establish is more useful than the slogan.** It built a coordinate-level registry of **candidate *cis*-regulatory elements (cCREs)**: ENCODE 3 (2020) published **926,535 human cCREs covering 7.9% of the genome**, and the 2025 expansion lists **~2.37 million**. That is a map you can look a patient's variant up in — which the 80% claim never was.

**Honest state of play:** far more than 1.5% of the genome does something; far less than 80% shows evidence of selected function. Anyone quoting either extreme as settled is over-claiming.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues humans must carry far more genes than a 1-mm nematode, because we are obviously more complex. What does the actual comparison show, and what does it imply?
options: The counts are similar (~19,400 vs ~20,000) — so complexity must come from regulation and splicing, not from the size of the parts list
Humans carry roughly ten times as many genes, which is exactly what complexity predicts
The nematode genome is physically larger, so it carries more genes
Gene counts cannot be compared across species with current methods
feedback: Correct — the near-parity is the whole point: information about cell identity is regulatory, not a longer parts list.
No — the counts are close. That mismatch between complexity and gene number is precisely what forced the field toward regulation.
No — genome size and gene count decouple badly. Some amoebas and plants have genomes far larger than ours with no complexity to match.
No — annotation is imperfect at the margins, but both counts are solid to within a few percent.

questions.prompt: A study reports that a stretch of intergenic DNA is transcribed at low level in one cell type. What has that established?
options: Only that the region is biochemically active — activity in one assay is not evidence of selection-maintained function
That it is a protein-coding gene the annotation missed
That it is junk DNA, since it produces no protein
That it is under purifying selection and therefore functional
feedback: Correct — this is exactly the conflation that sank the ENCODE '80% functional' headline.
No — transcription alone does not make a coding gene; you would need an open reading frame and evidence of translation.
No — the opposite error. Producing no protein says nothing either way; plenty of non-coding transcripts are regulatory.
No — selection is inferred from cross-species conservation or population constraint, not from a single transcription assay.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of the human genome is protein-coding exon, and roughly what fraction shows evidence of purifying selection?
options: ~1.5% coding; ~5–8% under selection
~1.5% coding; ~80% under selection
~25% coding; ~50% under selection
~50% coding, with the rest inert
feedback: Correct — and the gap between the two numbers is the regulatory genome.
No — 80% was the biochemical-activity figure, not the selection figure. Conflating them was the 2012 over-claim.
No — coding sequence is far smaller than that; ~1.5% is the well-established figure.
No — roughly half the genome is transposable-element derived, and coding sequence is a small fraction of the rest.

questions.prompt: Why did the last ~8% of the human genome stay unfinished from 2003 until 2022?
options: It is highly repetitive — centromeres, ribosomal DNA arrays, segmental duplications — so short reads cannot be placed uniquely
It was under legal and patent restriction until the mid-2010s
It contains no genes, so nobody was motivated to finish it
It had been sequenced but the raw data were lost
feedback: Correct — long reads (tens of kilobases) spanning whole repeat arrays were the enabling technology.
No — gene patents were a real controversy, but the 8% gap was a sequencing-technology limit, not a legal one.
No — the finished regions include ribosomal RNA gene arrays and centromeric sequence with real biology in them.
No — the sequence had never been read; that is what 'gap' meant.

concepts.title: From Gene to Protein — the central dogma, done properly
concepts.summary: Transcription, splicing, translation and folding — plus the part textbooks skip: where regulation actually lives, and why measuring mRNA does not tell you protein.

cards.h: Transcription and splicing — one gene, many messages
cards.md:
## DNA → *(transcription)* → pre-mRNA → *(splicing)* → mRNA → *(translation)* → polypeptide → *(folding)* → protein

**Transcription.** RNA polymerase II copies one DNA strand into **pre-mRNA** (precursor messenger RNA). The transcript gains a 5′ cap and a 3′ poly(A) tail — stability and export tags, not ornament.

**Splicing.** Human genes are interrupted. A typical gene spans **~27 kb** of DNA but contributes only **~1.3 kb** of protein-coding sequence, split across roughly 8–9 **exons** separated by **introns** — the intervening sequence, excised and discarded. The **spliceosome**, a large ribonucleoprotein machine, makes the cuts.

The crucial part: it does not always cut the same way. **~95% of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced** (Pan et al. and Wang et al., both 2008). Skip an exon, choose an alternative 5′ or 3′ splice site, retain an intron — and one gene yields many **isoforms**, sometimes with different or even opposing functions. That is how GENCODE gets **644,292 transcripts** out of ~19,400 coding genes.

Splicing is also a major disease mechanism. A variant buried deep in an intron that creates a new splice site can be as damaging as a nonsense variant in an exon — and standard **exome** sequencing, which reads only exons and their immediate flanks, will never see it.

cards.h: Translation and folding
cards.md:
**Translation.** The ribosome reads mRNA in **codons** — three bases per amino acid. Sixty-four codons encode 20 amino acids plus stop, so the code is **redundant**: several codons specify the same amino acid. tRNAs deliver the amino acids; the chain elongates at roughly 5–10 residues per second in human cells.

**Folding.** The chain is not a protein until it folds. Anfinsen's classic result — sequence determines structure — holds in the thermodynamic limit, but *in vivo* folding is **co-translational** (the N-terminal end begins folding before the C-terminal end exists) and **chaperone-assisted** (Hsp70, chaperonins). Rate matters: a **synonymous** codon change that alters translation speed can change the folded outcome without changing a single amino acid. 'Silent' variants are not reliably silent.

**What changed in the 2020s.** AlphaFold2 (2021) and its successors predict folded structure from sequence at near-experimental accuracy for most single domains, and a predicted structure now exists for essentially every human protein. Be precise about what that solved: it predicts the **endpoint**, not the folding pathway, not misfolding kinetics, and it is weakest exactly where biology gets interesting — intrinsically disordered regions, multi-chain complexes, and the stability effect of a single point substitution. Structure prediction did not become variant-effect prediction.

cards.h: Where regulation actually happens — and why protein ≠ mRNA
cards.md:
Regulation is a stack, not a step:

- **Promoter** — the launch pad immediately upstream where RNA Pol II assembles.
- **Enhancers** — short regulatory elements that can sit **hundreds of kilobases** away and act on a promoter by DNA looping. Loops are corralled inside **TADs** (topologically associating domains) bounded by CTCF and cohesin; delete a boundary and an enhancer can hijack the wrong gene — a documented disease mechanism.
- **Transcription factors (TFs)** — sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins. Humans have about **1,639** (Lambert et al., *Cell* 2018). Cell identity is a *combination* of TFs, not one master switch.
- **Chromatin** — DNA methylation and histone modification determine what is physically accessible at all.
- **Post-transcriptional** — splice choice, microRNA targeting, mRNA stability, translation-initiation rate.
- **Post-translational** — phosphorylation, ubiquitination and degradation, subcellular localisation.

**Hence: measuring mRNA does not tell you protein.** At steady state, mRNA abundance explains only about **40% of the variance** in protein abundance across genes (Liu, Beyer & Aebersold, *Cell* 2016), and considerably less during dynamic transitions. Median protein half-life (~46 h) far exceeds median mRNA half-life (~9 h) in mammalian cells, so protein levels integrate a history the transcript no longer reflects.

**Flagged as contested:** Csárdi and colleagues (2015) argued that measurement error deflates that correlation and the true steady-state relationship is much tighter (R² near 0.8). The disagreement is unresolved. What is *not* disputed: transcriptomics is a proxy for proteomics, never a substitute.

questions.prompt: A variant sits 200 bp deep inside an intron and changes no amino acid. A clinician calls it benign on that basis. What is the strongest counter-argument?
options: It can create or destroy a splice site, changing which exons reach the mRNA — and exome sequencing would not even have looked there
Introns are translated too, so it changes the protein directly
All intronic variants should be presumed pathogenic until proven otherwise
It would shorten the poly(A) tail and destabilise the transcript
feedback: Correct — deep-intronic splice-creating variants are a well-documented pathogenic class and a known blind spot of exome-only testing.
No — introns are excised before translation. The mechanism is splice disruption, not direct coding change.
No — the overwhelming majority of intronic variants are inert. The point is that 'intronic' does not settle the question either way.
No — poly(A) tail length is set at the 3′ end during cleavage and polyadenylation, not by a deep-intronic base change.

questions.prompt: An RNA-seq experiment shows a gene's mRNA doubled after treatment. What can you conclude about its protein?
options: Little on its own — mRNA explains only ~40% of the variance in protein levels at steady state, and less during transitions
The protein doubled as well, since translation output is proportional to message
The protein halved, because translational feedback inverts transcriptional changes
Nothing whatsoever can ever be inferred about protein from mRNA
feedback: Correct — it is evidence, not proof. Protein half-life, translation rate and degradation all sit between message and product.
No — proportionality is the assumption the proteomics data broke. Translation rate and protein turnover vary by orders of magnitude across genes.
No — there is no general inversion. Some genes are buffered, some track closely; direction is not systematically reversed.
No — this over-corrects. mRNA is genuinely informative, just far from sufficient; treat it as a proxy with a wide error bar.

questions.prompt: How do ~19,400 protein-coding genes produce hundreds of thousands of distinct transcripts?
options: Alternative splicing — about 95% of multi-exon genes are spliced in more than one way
Each gene is physically present in hundreds of tandem copies
The genetic code is redundant, so one gene specifies many different proteins
Ribosomes randomly skip codons, generating variant products
feedback: Correct — exon skipping, alternative splice-site choice and intron retention multiply one locus into many isoforms.
No — with a few exceptions such as ribosomal RNA and histone gene clusters, genes are single-copy.
No — redundancy means several codons specify the *same* amino acid. It reduces variety, it does not create isoforms.
No — ribosomal frameshifting exists but is a rare, programmed event, not a general source of transcript diversity.

questions.prompt: A synonymous ('silent') variant changes a codon but not the amino acid. Why might it still matter?
options: It can shift translation speed and therefore co-translational folding, or disrupt a splicing regulatory element inside the exon
It changes the amino acid after all, once the protein folds
Synonymous variants are consistently pathogenic and should be reported as such
It alters DNA methylation across the whole chromosome
feedback: Correct — codon usage tunes elongation rate, and exonic splicing enhancers and silencers sit inside coding sequence.
No — the amino acid is unchanged by definition; the effect is on the process, not the sequence of the product.
No — most synonymous variants really are inert. The point is that 'synonymous' is not automatic proof of benignity.
No — a single synonymous substitution does not remodel chromosome-wide methylation.

concepts.title: How Two Genomes Differ — the variation inventory
concepts.summary: Any two people differ at 4–5 million sites; almost none of it is coding, the structural-variant count depends on your sequencing platform, and roughly 70 differences per person are brand new.

cards.h: The inventory: 4–5 million differences, and what kind they are
cards.md:
Sequence any person and they differ from the reference at **4.1–5.0 million sites** (1000 Genomes Project, *Nature* 2015). That sounds enormous. It is about **0.1%** of 3.1 Gb.

By **count**, two classes dominate:

- **SNPs** — single-nucleotide polymorphisms, one base swapped for another. Roughly **4–4.5 million** per genome.
- **Indels** — short insertions or deletions under 50 bp. Roughly **600,000–800,000**.

Together those are **about 99.5% of the differing sites** — and that figure is itself platform-dependent, which is the point of the next card. Count structural variants the way short reads do (~2,300) and single-letter changes plus indels come to >99.9%; count them the way long reads do (~27,000) and it falls to ~99.5%. Same two genomes, same biology, different instrument. But measured in **bases affected**, the picture inverts. **Structural variants (SVs)** — anything ≥50 bp: deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations, and **copy-number variants (CNVs)**, where a whole segment is present in a different number of copies — touch on the order of **20 Mb** per genome despite being a rounding error by site count.

**Tandem repeats** are a category of their own: **short tandem repeats (STRs**, 2–6 bp motifs, ~1 million loci genome-wide) and **VNTRs** (variable-number tandem repeats, larger motifs). They mutate orders of magnitude faster than point sites, they are the basis of forensic DNA profiling, and pathological expansions cause roughly **60 known diseases** — Huntington's, fragile X, myotonic dystrophy, several ataxias and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis among them.

cards.h: How much of it is coding — and why the SV count keeps moving
cards.md:
**Coding is a sliver.** Of those 4–5 million differences, a typical genome carries roughly **10,000–12,000 sites that change a protein's amino-acid sequence**, and only **149–182 protein-truncating variants** — stop-gains, frameshifts, essential splice-site hits (1000 Genomes, 2015). So on the order of **0.3–0.5%** of your variants land in coding sequence at all, and only a couple of hundred are outright destructive.

Everything else is non-coding. That is why the regulatory map from the previous concept is not an academic aside — it is where most of the variation, and most of the GWAS signal, actually is.

**An honest caveat on the SV numbers.** They are as much a property of the instrument as of the biology. Short-read studies reported **~2,100–2,500 SVs per genome**. Haplotype-resolved **long-read** assemblies (Ebert et al., *Science* 2021) find **~23,000–31,000 per individual**, with roughly two-thirds invisible to short reads — overwhelmingly insertions in repetitive sequence, exactly where a 150-bp read cannot be anchored.

Read that as a general discipline: **'how many variants does a person carry' is a measurement-limited quantity.** Anyone quoting it without naming the platform is quoting an artefact of the technology as though it were a fact about people.

cards.h: 'Mutation' became 'variant' — and where new ones come from
cards.md:
**The vocabulary changed for a substantive reason.** The ACMG/AMP consensus standards (Richards et al., 2015 — American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, with the Association for Molecular Pathology) recommended retiring both **'mutation'** and **'polymorphism'** in favour of **'variant'**, qualified by an explicit five-tier call: **pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign, benign.**

The old words smuggled in conclusions. 'Mutation' had come to imply *disease-causing*; 'polymorphism' implied *harmless* and was often defined by a ≥1% frequency cut-off with **no biological basis** — plenty of common variants affect risk, plenty of rare ones are inert. Uptake was fast: about **89% of clinical laboratories** now avoid 'mutation' in reports. The residual problem is the **VUS** — most rare variants seen in a patient have no confident classification. That is much of why **gnomAD** exists (**807,162 individuals**: 730,947 exomes plus 76,215 genomes). A variant found in thousands of healthy adults cannot be a highly penetrant cause of severe early-onset disease.

**De novo variants.** Some of your differences are brand new — present in you and in neither parent. Across 1,548 Icelandic parent–offspring trios the average was **70.3 de novo point mutations per child** (Jónsson et al., *Nature* 2017). About **80% arise on the paternal chromosome**, because spermatogonial precursors keep dividing for life while oocytes do not.

Hence the **paternal-age effect**, quantified: **+1.51 mutations per year of the father's age** versus **+0.37 per year of the mother's** — roughly *doubling* the de novo count between a 20-year-old and a 40-year-old father. It is a real contributor to sporadic dominant disorders. Keep the magnitude honest, though: the *relative* increase for specific conditions is meaningful, while the *absolute* risk to any individual older father's child stays small.

questions.prompt: Two labs sequence the same person. Lab A (short reads) reports ~2,300 structural variants; Lab B (long reads) reports ~27,000. Which is right?
options: Both report what their platform can resolve — long reads detect insertions in repetitive sequence that short reads cannot anchor
Lab B is wrong; the established true figure is ~2,300 per genome
Lab A is wrong; it discarded real calls to hit a target number
Neither — the person's genome changed between the two runs
feedback: Correct — the ~3× discrepancy is a detection-sensitivity artefact, which is why the platform belongs in any quoted figure.
No — the ~2,300 figure was itself a floor set by short-read sensitivity, not a biological ceiling.
No — short-read pipelines are not discarding calls; they cannot place reads inside long repeats in the first place.
No — the germline genome is stable across a blood draw; somatic change is far too small to explain a 10× gap.

questions.prompt: You carry roughly 4–5 million variants. About how many change a protein's amino-acid sequence?
options: About 10,000–12,000, of which only ~150–180 actually truncate a protein
Roughly half of them — coding sequence is where variation concentrates
About 2 million, split evenly between coding and non-coding
None — coding sequence is invariant between healthy people
feedback: Correct — on the order of 0.3–0.5% of your variants are coding, which is why non-coding interpretation is the hard problem.
No — coding sequence is only ~1.5% of the genome and is under stronger purifying selection, so it carries proportionally less variation.
No — that is off by roughly two orders of magnitude for amino-acid-altering sites.
No — healthy people routinely carry ~150 protein-truncating variants, most in genes tolerant of loss.

questions.prompt: Why did ACMG/AMP push the field from 'mutation' and 'polymorphism' to 'variant' plus a five-tier classification?
options: Both old terms pre-judged pathogenicity, and the 1%-frequency line defining 'polymorphism' has no biological justification
The word 'mutation' tested badly with patients but the science was unaffected
Because variants are a distinct molecular class from mutations
Because the five tiers removed uncertainty from variant interpretation
feedback: Correct — the terminology was carrying a conclusion that the evidence had not yet earned.
No — patient communication mattered, but the driver was that the terms encoded unjustified claims about effect.
No — they describe the same molecular objects; the difference was only in the implied interpretation.
No — the opposite. The tiers made uncertainty explicit by creating the 'variant of uncertain significance' category.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old man and a 25-year-old man each father a child. Predict the difference in de novo point mutations, and what it does and does not mean.
options: Roughly 30 more in the older father's child (~+1.5 per year) — a genuine contributor to sporadic dominant disease, but the absolute risk to any one child stays small
No difference — the de novo mutation rate per generation is constant
About 3,000 more, which makes fathering children after 40 medically inadvisable
Fewer, because ageing sperm undergo stronger selection before fertilisation
feedback: Correct — +1.51/year over 20 years is ~30 mutations, roughly doubling the paternal contribution, with a small absolute effect per child.
No — the rate rises measurably with paternal age because spermatogonia keep dividing throughout life.
No — the slope is ~1.5 per year, not ~150. Over-stating the magnitude is as misleading as denying the effect.
No — the effect runs the other way: more precursor cell divisions means more replication errors, not fewer.

concepts.title: Mendelian Inheritance — and the two things that break it
concepts.summary: Dominant, recessive and X-linked patterns predict transmission reliably; penetrance and expressivity are why they predict outcome only probabilistically.

cards.h: The patterns you actually meet
cards.md:
**Autosomal dominant** — one altered copy on an autosome (a non-sex chromosome) suffices. An affected parent transmits to **50%** of offspring, and the pedigree runs vertically through generations. Examples: **Huntington's disease** (a CAG repeat expansion in *HTT*); **familial hypercholesterolemia** (~**1 in 250** people — commoner than most clinicians assume).

**Autosomal recessive** — **both** copies must be altered. Two unaffected carriers face a **25%** risk per pregnancy, and the pedigree looks horizontal: siblings affected, parents not. Example: **cystic fibrosis** (*CFTR*), carrier frequency ~1 in 25 in Northern European ancestry, ~1 in 2,500–3,500 births.

**X-linked** — males are **hemizygous** (one X), so a single altered copy is fully expressed: **haemophilia A** (*F8*), **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** (*DMD*, ~1 in 5,000 male births). Female carriers are **mosaics**, because X-inactivation silences one X at random in each cell early in development. So 'carrier' is not a synonym for 'unaffected' — skewed inactivation leaves a minority of carriers genuinely symptomatic.

**Mitochondrial** — transmitted only from the mother, and complicated by **heteroplasmy**: a mixture of normal and altered mitochondrial genomes within one cell. Severity tracks mutant load, not a clean genotype.

**Compound heterozygosity** cuts across all of the recessive cases and is the common real-world situation: **two *different* pathogenic variants, one on each copy** of the gene. In cystic fibrosis, F508del homozygotes are only about **45%** of patients; most of the rest are compound heterozygotes. Practical consequence: a report saying 'one pathogenic *CFTR* variant found' has excluded one allele, not the disease.

cards.h: Penetrance — and the BRCA1 number that fell
cards.md:
**Penetrance** is the probability that a carrier of a genotype develops the phenotype. Naive Mendelism assumes 100%. Almost nothing is.

Even Huntington's, the textbook fully penetrant dominant, is graded by repeat length: **≥40 CAG repeats** is effectively fully penetrant; **36–39** is *reduced* penetrance — carriers who may never manifest.

**The instructive case is BRCA1, because the number moved a long way and the reason is methodological, not biological.**

- **1990s, Breast Cancer Linkage Consortium** — families selected *because* they were loaded with cancer: breast-cancer risk **~85% by age 70**.
- **Antoniou et al., 2003** — meta-analysis of 22 case series *unselected for family history*: **65% (BRCA1)**, **45% (BRCA2)** by 70.
- **Kuchenbaecker et al., *JAMA* 2017** — prospective cohort: **72% (BRCA1)**, **69% (BRCA2)** by age **80**; ovarian 44% and 17%.
- **Jackson et al., *eClinicalMedicine* 2023 — UK Biobank, population-ascertained:** BRCA1 breast-cancer penetrance by age 60 was **44.7% in women with a first-degree family history but only 22.8% in women without**.

The driver is **ascertainment bias**. You discover a gene by studying families full of the disease, so the founding penetrance estimate is implicitly *conditioned on* that family history — and it silently carries whatever shared modifier alleles and environment made those families conspicuous in the first place.

**The clinical consequence is concrete:** a *BRCA1* pathogenic variant found incidentally in a healthy woman with no family history does **not** carry the 72% figure. Note also that this debate is live — the UK Biobank estimates themselves drew published rebuttals (*BJC Reports*, 2024) over healthy-volunteer bias and censoring. Here the honest answer is a range plus a statement of how the person was ascertained, not a single number.

cards.h: Expressivity — and why 'Mendelian' is really a spectrum
cards.md:
**Penetrance is *whether*. Expressivity is *how much*.** Two carriers of the *same* variant, in the *same* family, can differ enormously in severity and in which organs are involved.

**Neurofibromatosis type 1** (*NF1*, ~1 in 3,000) is the standard illustration: penetrance is near-complete, yet one sibling has a few café-au-lait macules while the next has disfiguring plexiform neurofibromas, optic glioma and learning disability — same variant, same household.

Four forces break the clean genotype→phenotype map:

1. **Modifier genes.** In cystic fibrosis, lung-disease severity among identical *CFTR* genotypes tracks unlinked modifier loci.
2. **Polygenic background.** Common-variant polygenic risk scores measurably shift risk *within* carrier groups — the same *BRCA2* variant means different things on different genomic backgrounds.
3. **Somatic and stochastic events.** X-inactivation skew, a second somatic hit, developmental noise. Monozygotic twins discordant for a 'Mendelian' phenotype are the proof.
4. **Environment and sex.** Hormonal milieu, diet, exposures, and sex-limited expression.

Repeat-expansion disorders add **anticipation** — the repeat tends to grow on transmission, so onset comes earlier and severity worsens down a pedigree. The molecular phenomenon is real, but the historical clinical claims of anticipation were badly inflated by ascertainment bias, so treat the term with the same scepticism as a penetrance figure.

**The usable summary:** Mendelian inheritance predicts **transmission** well — the 50%, 25% and X-linked ratios hold. It predicts **outcome** only probabilistically. Genotype is a strong prior, not a verdict.

questions.prompt: Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What is the recurrence risk for their next pregnancy, and why?
options: 25% — both parents must be carriers, and each pregnancy is an independent draw
0% — the family's risk was used up by the affected child
50%, as with any single-gene condition in a family
100%, since both parents are established carriers
feedback: Correct — carrier × carrier gives 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% neither, independently at every conception.
No — this is the gambler's fallacy applied to meiosis. Prior outcomes do not change the next segregation.
No — 50% is the transmission risk for an affected parent with a dominant condition, not for two recessive carriers.
No — carriers each transmit the altered allele half the time, so both must coincide: 0.5 × 0.5 = 25%.

questions.prompt: A symptomatic patient's panel reports one pathogenic CFTR variant. Has cystic fibrosis been excluded?
options: No — most non-F508del patients are compound heterozygotes, and the second allele may be a variant the panel does not cover
Yes — one variant means carrier status by definition
Yes, because CFTR disease requires two copies of the same variant
No, because CFTR is X-linked and one copy is sufficient in males
feedback: Correct — targeted panels cover common variants; a rare second allele (including deep-intronic or structural) needs full gene sequencing to find.
No — that inference only holds if the second allele has actually been ruled out, which a limited panel cannot do.
No — the two pathogenic alleles need not be identical. Compound heterozygosity is the majority of non-F508del disease.
No — CFTR is on chromosome 7 and is autosomal recessive; the reasoning is wrong even though the conclusion is right.

questions.prompt: A healthy 35-year-old woman with no family history of cancer learns incidentally that she carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. What risk figure should she be quoted?
options: Lower than the clinic-cohort 72%-by-80 figure — population-ascertained data put risk by 60 near 23% without family history versus ~45% with one
72% by age 80 — the published figure applies to every carrier regardless of how she was found
The population baseline of ~13%, since she has no family history
Zero, because penetrance requires a family history to be expressed
feedback: Correct — this is the practical payoff of understanding ascertainment bias, and the honest answer is a range plus how she was ascertained.
No — that figure comes from cohorts enriched for family history; applying it to an incidental finding over-states her risk.
No — this over-corrects. Her risk is clearly elevated above baseline; it is the size of the elevation that shifts.
No — carriers without family history still show markedly elevated risk, roughly 23% by age 60 in UK Biobank.

questions.prompt: Two brothers carry the identical NF1 variant. One has a few café-au-lait macules; the other has plexiform neurofibromas and optic glioma. What is this, and what explains it?
options: Variable expressivity — modifier genes, polygenic background, somatic and stochastic events, and environment
Incomplete penetrance — the mildly affected brother must not actually carry the variant
Non-paternity, which is the usual explanation for discordant siblings
A misdiagnosis — identical variants necessarily produce identical phenotypes
feedback: Correct — both are affected (so penetrance is intact); the variation is in severity, which is expressivity.
No — he does carry it and he is affected, just mildly. Incomplete penetrance would mean no phenotype at all.
No — both brothers carry the same confirmed variant, so shared inheritance is not in question.
No — this is precisely the assumption that variable expressivity refutes; NF1 is the classic counterexample.

resources.note: Side-by-side table of all eight inheritance patterns with worked examples — the cleanest reference for the non-specialist.

resources.note: The prospective-cohort penetrance estimates (72% / 69% by age 80) with confidence intervals — one end of the ascertainment story.

concepts.title: Polygenic Traits and the Heritability Trap
concepts.summary: Most human traits are built from thousands of loci of small additive effect, which is why they form bell curves instead of Mendel's discrete classes — and why heritability (h²), a population-level variance ratio, is the most misread number in all of genetics.

cards.h: Why Mendel's peas don't look like people
cards.md:
Gregor Mendel picked traits governed by **one locus** (one position in the genome) with two clearly distinguishable alleles — round versus wrinkled, tall versus short. Those give **discrete classes** in fixed ratios. Human height, blood pressure, cholesterol and essentially every disease risk do not behave that way. They form smooth, roughly bell-shaped distributions.

**Ronald Fisher** dissolved the apparent contradiction in 1918: a continuous distribution is exactly what you get from *adding up many* Mendelian loci of small effect.

Take a toy trait with **3 loci**, two alleles each, every allele at frequency 0.5, each "plus" allele adding the same fixed increment. A person carries 6 alleles, so the genotype score *k* runs 0 to 6. Under independent assortment the class sizes are the binomial coefficients:

## k = 0,1,2,3,4,5,6 → 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1  out of 64

Three loci already give seven classes and a hump in the middle: the modal class (*k* = 3) holds 20/64 ≈ 31% of people, each extreme holds 1/64 ≈ 1.6%. Go to 100 loci and you have 201 classes, spaced so finely that ordinary measurement error smears them into a continuum. The **central limit theorem** finishes the job: sums of many small independent contributions converge on the normal distribution whatever the shape of each contribution.

Watch what happens to the tails. With *n* loci each contributing effect *a*, the full range is 2*na* while the standard deviation grows only as *a*√(n/2), so

## range ÷ SD = 2√(2n)

At *n* = 100 that is 28 standard deviations. Carrying *every* plus allele is not merely rare, it is effectively impossible. Extremes in a polygenic trait come from the shoulders of a very wide distribution, never from one special genotype.

cards.h: Heritability, defined the way a geneticist means it
cards.md:
**Heritability** is a ratio of variances, not a property of a person. Partition the observed (phenotypic) variance in a population:

## Vₚ = V_G + V_E    and    V_G = V_A + V_D + V_I

- **V_A** — *additive* genetic variance: the part that behaves like the toy model above, where each allele contributes an increment that simply sums.
- **V_D** — *dominance* variance: interaction between the two alleles at the same locus.
- **V_I** — *epistatic* variance: interaction between loci.
- **V_E** — environmental variance: everything non-genetic, including measurement noise and developmental accident.

Two heritabilities follow:

## H² (broad-sense) = V_G / Vₚ        h² (narrow-sense) = V_A / Vₚ

**h²** is the one that does practical work, because only additive variance is reliably transmitted parent to offspring. That is why the breeder's equation — response *R* to a selection differential *S* — is **R = h²S**, not H²S. A striking empirical regularity: even when the underlying biology is full of dominance and epistasis, *most* of the genetic variance in real populations turns out to be additive, because interaction effects at realistic allele frequencies mostly project onto the additive term.

The classical estimator from twins uses Falconer's formula, where *r* is the trait correlation within monozygotic (identical) and dizygotic (fraternal) twin pairs:

## h² ≈ 2(r_MZ − r_DZ) = 2(0.90 − 0.45) = 0.90

For height, twin studies land near **0.7–0.8**. Molecular methods land lower: the 2022 saturated height map of 5.4 million people (Yengo et al., *Nature*) found **12,111** independent genome-wide-significant variants explaining about **40%** of height variance in European-ancestry samples.

Be honest about the twin number. It assumes identical and fraternal twins share environments equally, and it quietly absorbs assortative mating and gene–environment correlation into the genetic bucket. Twin h² estimates are best read as **upper bounds**, not measurements.

cards.h: ★ Five things h² does not mean
cards.md:
This is the most misused number in genetics. The negatives are where the teaching is.

**1. Not "how much of your trait is genetic."** h² = 0.8 for height does *not* mean 80% of your height came from genes and 20% from food. It means that in *this* population, in *these* environments, 80% of the *variance between people* tracks additive genetic differences. Any one person's height is 100% genes and 100% environment; neither is optional, and a variance ratio cannot be applied to an individual at all.

**2. Not a constant of the trait.** Change the population or the environmental range and h² changes. Number of fingers is under near-total genetic specification, yet its heritability is close to **zero** — nearly all the variance in finger count comes from accidents, not alleles.

**3. Not a limit on intervention.** Height's h² is high, and South Korean women born in 1996 were **20.2 cm** taller than those born in 1896 (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, *eLife* 2016) — roughly three population standard deviations, from nutrition and infection control, with no change in allele frequencies. **Phenylketonuria (PKU)**, a single-gene disorder with heritability near 1, is almost entirely prevented by a low-phenylalanine diet.

Worse for the intuition: a *successful, universal* intervention **raises** h², because it strips environmental variance out of the denominator.

## h² = V_A / (V_A + V_E),  so  V_E ↓  ⇒  h² ↑

Equalise schooling and the heritability of test scores goes *up*. High heritability is evidence that environments are already similar — not that they are powerless.

**4. Says nothing about differences between groups.** Richard Lewontin's parable: split one bag of genetically variable seed between a rich pot and a poor pot. Within each pot every difference in plant height is genetic (h² = 1). Between pots every difference is soil. High within-group heritability is fully compatible with a 100%-environmental between-group gap. The two questions are logically independent.

**5. Names no gene.** A heritability estimate is a variance accounting. It identifies no locus, no mechanism and no target.

questions.prompt: In the 3-locus toy model (two alleles per locus, every allele at frequency 0.5, each 'plus' allele adding the same increment), what fraction of the population carries the maximum score of 6 plus alleles?
options: 1 in 64 (about 1.6%)
1 in 6 (about 17%)
20 in 64 (about 31%)
feedback: Correct — six alleles, each independently plus-or-minus at frequency 0.5, give 2⁶ = 64 equally likely combinations, and exactly one of them is all-plus. The weights 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 are a bell curve in embryo.
1 in 8 is the answer for three coin flips, not six. Each locus contributes two alleles, so the score runs 0 to 6 across 2⁶ = 64 equally likely combinations, only one of which is all-plus.
1 in 6 confuses a count of alleles with a probability. The all-plus genotype is one outcome out of the 2⁶ = 64 equally likely allele draws, not one out of six.
20 out of 64 is the modal class — three plus alleles, the middle of the distribution. The extreme is the opposite case, the rarest class at 1 in 64.

questions.prompt: A country eliminates childhood malnutrition. Over two generations mean adult height rises 6 cm. What happens to the heritability of height in that country?
options: It falls, because the environment has just proved it is doing the work
It rises, because removing environmental variance shrinks the denominator
It stays the same — heritability is a property of the trait
It becomes undefined once the population mean shifts
feedback: This inverts the mechanism. Eliminating malnutrition removes a source of variation *between people*, so V_E falls. Since h² = V_A/(V_A+V_E), a smaller V_E makes the ratio larger, not smaller.

Correct, and this is the counterintuitive heart of the concept. h² = V_A/(V_A+V_E), so a successful universal intervention removes environmental variance and heritability rises — even though the environment just moved the population mean by 6 cm.
Heritability is not a property of the trait. It is a property of a particular population in a particular range of environments, and it moves whenever either one moves.
Heritability is a variance ratio and remains perfectly well defined after a shift in the mean. What changed here is the variance decomposition, not the definition.

questions.prompt: A study reports h² = 0.75 for adult body mass index in a Danish cohort. Which statement is correct?
options: In that population and environment, 75% of the variance in body mass index between people tracks additive genetic differences
75% of any given Dane's body mass index is caused by their genes
Diet and activity can change body mass index by at most 25%
75% of Danes carry an obesity-predisposing gene
feedback: Correct — heritability is a population-level variance ratio, conditional on the environments actually present in that sample. It is a statement about differences between people, never about the composition of one person.

This is the individual-level fallacy. A variance ratio cannot be applied to a single person; your body mass index does not decompose into a genetic 75% and an environmental 25%. Both causes are entirely necessary.
Heritability places no bound on what intervention can achieve. Height has a comparable h² and rose by roughly three population standard deviations in a century on nutrition alone.
Heritability names no gene and counts no carriers. It is a variance accounting, not an allele frequency.

questions.prompt: Two groups are raised in systematically different environments. Within each group the heritability of a trait is 0.9. The group means differ by 5 points. What can you conclude about the cause of the between-group gap?
options: Nothing — within-group heritability carries no information about between-group causes
That about 90% of the gap is genetic
That the gap must be entirely environmental
That the trait must be Mendelian
feedback: Correct — Lewontin's two-pots parable makes exactly this point: identical seed in rich and poor soil gives h² = 1 within each pot and a 100% environmental gap between them. Within-group and between-group questions are logically independent.

This is the most common misuse of heritability in public argument. A within-group variance decomposition is silent about between-group means; two pots can differ entirely because of soil while heritability inside each pot is 1.0.
Also unwarranted on this evidence. The data given cannot establish an environmental cause either — the honest answer is that within-group h² is simply uninformative here.
High heritability is entirely compatible with thousands of loci of tiny effect. Mendelian inheritance is a claim about one locus producing discrete classes, which nothing here implies.

resources.label: Visscher, Hill & Wray (2008), "Heritability in the genomics era — concepts and misconceptions," Nature Reviews Genetics
resources.note: The canonical correction of every misconception on the third card, written by the people who build the estimators. If you read one thing after this concept, read this.

concepts.title: GWAS: What a Million Regressions Can and Cannot Tell You
concepts.summary: A genome-wide association study runs one regression per variant across the genome, which forces a significance threshold of 5×10⁻⁸ and yields thousands of hits with odds ratios near 1.1 — associations that are usually tags for something nearby, and almost never a 'gene for' anything.

cards.h: One regression per variant — and the price of that many tests
cards.md:
A **genome-wide association study (GWAS)** genotypes a large cohort on an array reading roughly 500,000 to 1,000,000 pre-chosen **single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs** — single-letter positions where people commonly differ), imputes up to ~10 million more from a reference panel, then runs one regression per variant:

## y = μ + β·x + (ancestry covariates),   x ∈ {0, 1, 2}

where *x* counts copies of the tested allele and *y* is the trait. Out comes one β and one p-value per variant. That is the whole method: a very large, very shallow scan for **association**.

Now the price of that many tests. At the conventional α = 0.05, a million tests would deliver

## 0.05 × 1,000,000 = 50,000 false positives

burying any real signal. The **Bonferroni** correction divides α by the number of *independent* tests. Common SNPs are not independent — neighbours travel together — and empirical work put the effective number of independent common-variant tests in European-ancestry genomes at roughly one million. Hence the field-wide threshold:

## α = 0.05 / 1,000,000 = 5 × 10⁻⁸   (|z| = 5.45, χ²₁ = 29.7)

Two honest caveats. **First**, African-ancestry genomes carry shorter blocks of co-inherited DNA and therefore *more* independent tests, so 5×10⁻⁸ is too lenient there; thresholds nearer 1×10⁻⁸ have been proposed. The "universal" threshold is calibrated to European ancestry, like much else in this field.

**Second**, a stringent p-value buys you nothing against confounding. **Population stratification** — ancestry correlating with both allele frequency and trait — survives the standard defences of genotype principal components and mixed models. In 2019 two *eLife* papers (Berg et al.; Sohail et al.) showed the celebrated signal of natural selection on height across Europe largely dissolved once better-controlled data replaced the original consortium estimates. And within-sibship GWAS, which compares siblings and so controls ancestry exactly, found effect estimates for educational attainment roughly **40% smaller** than population estimates (Howe et al., 2022).

cards.h: Effect sizes are tiny, and that sets the sample size
cards.md:
Typical common-variant hits are small. For disease, **odds ratios (OR** — the odds of disease in carriers divided by the odds in non-carriers) cluster in the **1.05 to 1.20** range. Translate one into absolute terms. Take a disease with 5% baseline risk and a variant with OR = 1.10:

## odds = 0.05/0.95 = 0.0526 → ×1.10 = 0.0579 → risk = 0.0579/1.0579 = 5.5%

A "10% increase in odds" moves absolute risk by **half a percentage point**. Headline-sized language, rounding-error consequences.

For a quantitative trait the arithmetic is just as sobering. A typical genome-wide-significant height variant shifts adult height by about **1 mm per allele**. Height's standard deviation is roughly 7 cm, so β ≈ 0.1/7 = 0.014 standard deviations. The variance explained by one such variant at minor allele frequency *p* = 0.3 is

## V = 2pq·β² = 2(0.3)(0.7)(0.014²) = 0.42 × 1.96×10⁻⁴ ≈ 8×10⁻⁵

That is **0.008%** of the variance. You would need roughly 5,000 such variants to reach 40% — and Yengo et al. (2022) found 12,111.

Now the power calculation that explains the entire history of the field. The chi-square test statistic's non-centrality parameter is λ = N·2pq·β². Clearing 5×10⁻⁸ requires χ²₁ > 29.7, and 80% power requires λ ≈ (5.45 + 0.84)² ≈ 39.6. Therefore

## N = 39.6 / (8×10⁻⁵) ≈ 480,000 participants

That is why GWAS sample sizes marched from a few thousand in 2007 to 5.4 million by 2022. The threshold is not bureaucracy — it *is* the sample-size requirement. It is also why the pre-GWAS era of small candidate-gene studies produced a decade of claims that would not replicate: at N = 1,000 those studies had essentially no power to detect anything real, so almost everything they reported at p < 0.05 was noise.

cards.h: The hit is a signpost, not the culprit — and where the heritability went
cards.md:
**Linkage disequilibrium (LD)** is the tendency of alleles at nearby positions to be inherited together as a block, because recombination rarely separates them. An array does not test the causal variant; it tests whichever variant it happens to carry a probe for, and that variant lights up if it sits in the same LD block. The reported "lead SNP" is therefore usually a **tag** — correlated with the cause, not the cause.

Two consequences kill the "gene for X" headline:

- More than **90%** of GWAS hits fall in non-coding DNA — regulatory sequence, not protein-coding genes. Reports name the *nearest* gene as a labelling convention, and that convention is often wrong. The famous obesity association inside an intron of **FTO** turned out to act on **IRX3** and **IRX5**, genes hundreds of kilobases away. Every headline that said "the FTO obesity gene" was naming the signpost, not the culprit.
- Effect sizes are so small that no single variant is a "gene for" anything. Sitting in the top decile of a thousand-variant score is a claim about a distribution, not a diagnosis.

**Missing heritability.** Twin studies put height's h² near 0.8. In 2010 the genome-wide-significant variants explained about 5%. Whole-genome methods that fit all common SNPs at once recovered roughly 45%; by 2022, with 5.4 million participants, the significant variants themselves reached 40% — in European-ancestry samples, and only 10–20% in others. The gap closed along four routes: thousands of real variants sitting *below* the threshold, imperfect tagging of causal variants by array SNPs, rare variants that arrays never see, and the uncomfortable fourth — that twin h² was **inflated to begin with** by assortative mating and shared environment.

Treat the residual gap as unresolved. How much of it is real biology and how much is an overstated denominator is still argued in the literature, and anyone who quotes a tidy number is skipping the argument.

questions.prompt: Why is the GWAS significance threshold 5×10⁻⁸ rather than the conventional 0.05?
options: Because Bonferroni divides α = 0.05 by roughly one million effectively independent common-variant tests
Because genetics demands more certainty than other fields, by disciplinary convention
Because genetic effect sizes are unusually large and deserve a stricter bar
Because 5×10⁻⁸ is the measured false-discovery rate of the human genome
feedback: Correct — 0.05/10⁶ = 5×10⁻⁸. The count is one million rather than ten million because linkage disequilibrium makes neighbouring SNPs redundant, so the effective number of independent tests is far below the number of variants actually tested.

It is not a taste for rigour. Run a million tests at α = 0.05 and you expect 50,000 false positives — the threshold is arithmetic forced by the number of tests, and any field running a million tests would need the same correction.
The opposite is true: common-variant effect sizes are tiny (odds ratios near 1.1). Small effects plus a stringent threshold are exactly what forces GWAS sample sizes into the hundreds of thousands.
A false-discovery rate is a property of a study's results, not a constant of the genome. 5×10⁻⁸ is a family-wise error rate derived by Bonferroni correction.

questions.prompt: A variant has an odds ratio of 1.10 for a disease whose baseline risk is 5%. A carrier's absolute risk is approximately:
feedback: 15% would require roughly a threefold increase in risk. An odds ratio of 1.10 is a 10% increase in the odds, not a tripling of the probability.
Correct — odds = 0.05/0.95 = 0.0526, times 1.10 = 0.0579, converted back to a probability = 0.0579/1.0579 ≈ 5.5%. A 10% relative bump on a small baseline is half a percentage point in absolute terms.
50% confuses the odds ratio with a probability. An odds ratio multiplies the odds; it is not itself a risk level.
10% would be a doubling of risk, corresponding to an odds ratio near 2.1, not 1.10. Multiplying the odds by 1.10 moves absolute risk from 5.0% to about 5.5%.

questions.prompt: A GWAS reports a genome-wide-significant SNP inside an intron of the FTO gene, associated with body mass index. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: FTO is the obesity gene
The SNP tags a linkage-disequilibrium block; the causal element may be regulatory sequence acting on a different gene entirely
Carrying the allele causes obesity in most carriers
The finding is probably a false positive, because the variant is non-coding
feedback: This is precisely the headline that follow-up work refuted. The FTO intronic signal was traced to a regulatory element acting on IRX3 and IRX5, hundreds of kilobases away. The nearest gene is a naming convention, not a mechanism.

Correct — over 90% of GWAS hits are non-coding, and the lead SNP is usually a tag correlated with the causal element through linkage disequilibrium. Fine-mapping and functional experiments are required to name the actual actor.

Common-variant effect sizes are tiny — this variant shifts body mass index by a fraction of a unit. The overwhelming majority of carriers are unaffected; the signal is a small shift in a population distribution.
Non-coding location is not evidence against a finding — it is the norm. Most of the genome's regulatory machinery lies outside protein-coding sequence, which is why so many hits land there.

questions.prompt: Twin studies put height's heritability near 0.8, but by 2010 the genome-wide-significant variants explained only about 5% of the variance. Which is NOT a credible contributor to that gap?
options: Thousands of real variants sitting just below the significance threshold
Rare variants that genotyping arrays do not cover
Twin-study heritability being inflated by assortative mating and shared environment
A small number of undiscovered large-effect common variants that determine height
feedback: This is a genuine contributor, and it turned out to be the largest. Raising the sample size to 5.4 million lifted the significant variants' share of height variance from 5% to about 40%.
Genuine — arrays genotype common variants by design, so rare and structural variation is largely invisible to them. Whole-genome sequencing recovers part of it.

Genuine, and the least comfortable of the four. Twin estimates assume identical and fraternal twins share environments equally and absorb assortative mating into the genetic term, so they behave as upper bounds.

Correct as the odd one out — this was the original hope and it failed. Two decades of scanning found no small set of large-effect common variants for height; the architecture is thousands of loci of very small effect.

resources.label: NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog
resources.note: The curated registry of published associations, searchable by trait, gene or variant, with full summary statistics. Look up any 'gene for X' headline here and read the actual odds ratio.
