concepts.title: Polygenic Risk Scores: Real Signal, Small Print
concepts.summary: A polygenic risk score is a weighted sum of risk alleles read as a percentile; it genuinely stratifies populations — a top-decile coronary score carries risk comparable to familial hypercholesterolemia — but it loses roughly fivefold accuracy outside European ancestry, ranks individuals barely better than a coin flip, and reports relative risks that usually mean small absolute changes.

cards.h: How the score is built, and what the number is
cards.md:
A **polygenic risk score (PRS**, also called a polygenic score or PGS) collapses a whole genome into one number:

## PRSᵢ = Σⱼ βⱼ · xᵢⱼ

Here *xᵢⱼ* is the count (0, 1 or 2) of the effect allele at variant *j* in person *i*, and *βⱼ* is the effect estimate borrowed from a GWAS — a log-odds for disease traits. Early scores used only genome-wide-significant hits. Modern methods (LDpred, PRS-CS) use **millions** of variants with statistically shrunken weights, precisely because most of the signal sits below the significance threshold. As of mid-2026 the PGS Catalog lists roughly **7,000** published scores across about **800** traits.

The raw sum has no interpretable units — it is a sum of log-odds against an arbitrary reference. So it is standardised against a **reference panel** and reported as a percentile, or in standard deviations from that panel's mean.

That standardisation step carries the entire ancestry problem inside it. Your percentile is defined relative to whoever is in the panel. Allele frequencies differ systematically between populations, so comparing an African-ancestry genome against a European-ancestry panel produces a percentile that describes the mismatch between the two, not the person.

Be clear about what a PRS is *not*. It is not a test for a variant — no specific allele is being reported as yours. It is not a diagnosis, and it has no defined positive predictive value for an individual. And it is not modifiable: your score is fixed at conception, while most of the risk it estimates is not.

cards.h: What it genuinely does — and the relative-versus-absolute trap
cards.md:
The real capability is **population stratification**: sorting a population into risk strata that clinical variables miss.

Khera et al. (*Nature Genetics*, 2018) built a genome-wide score for coronary artery disease and found it identified **8.0% of the population** at more than **threefold** increased risk — comparable to carrying a **familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)** variant, the classic single-gene cause of premature heart disease. FH affects roughly 1 in 250 people. So the score flags about **twenty times more** high-risk individuals than FH screening does, including people whom family history and standard risk factors missed entirely. That result is real and it replicates.

Now the trap. Relative risk is dimensionless; decisions live in absolute units.

Take a 50-year-old man whose 10-year coronary event risk on standard clinical factors is 5%. Put him in a top-decile stratum carrying 2× relative risk:

## 2.0 × 5% = 10%  →  absolute increase of 5 percentage points

That is a genuine conversation about a statin. Now take a 35-year-old whose 10-year baseline is 0.5% — same decile, same 2×:

## 2.0 × 0.5% = 1.0%  →  absolute increase of 0.5 percentage points

Identical headline — "your genetic risk is doubled" — and one is worth acting on while the other is noise. Note also what the 10% figure implies for the 50-year-old: **90 of every 100 people in that top decile have no event in ten years.** A doubled risk is still, overwhelmingly, an uneventful decade. Always ask for the two absolute numbers, not the ratio between them.

cards.h: ★ Three limits, one of them severe
cards.md:
**1. Ancestry portability — the severe one.** Scores are trained where the data are, and Martin et al. (*Nature Genetics*, 2019) reported that **79% of GWAS participants were of European descent**, a group that is 16% of the world's population. Their measured consequence, relative to European-ancestry performance:

## accuracy 1.6× lower (Hispanic/Latino) · 1.7× (South Asian) · 2.5× (East Asian) · 4.9× lower (African ancestry)

The mechanism is not mysterious. Allele frequencies differ and linkage-disequilibrium blocks differ, so a tag variant that proxies a causal variant in one population may not proxy it in another. Concretely: the 12,111 height variants from the 2022 saturated map explain about **40%** of height variance in European-ancestry samples and only **10–20%** elsewhere. A 2023 *Nature* analysis (Ding et al.) showed accuracy decays **continuously** with genetic distance from the training sample — so "ancestry-matched" labelling is a crude patch on a continuous problem, and accuracy varies even inside a labelled group.

**2. Individual discrimination is weak even where the population signal is real.** Elliott et al. (*JAMA*, 2020; N = 352,660) measured the C-statistic for incident coronary artery disease: **0.61** for the polygenic score alone, **0.76** for the clinical pooled cohort equations, **0.78** for both combined. A C-statistic of 0.61 means: draw one person who will have an event and one who will not, and the score ranks them in the right order **61%** of the time — against 50% for a coin flip. Its *incremental* value over cheap clinical variables was about **0.02**.

**3. A population tool is being sold as an individual one.** A score that shifts a cohort's mean risk is not a score that tells one person what will happen. Commercial embryo-selection scores extrapolate far past this evidence base, and the major genetics societies do not support that use.

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old woman's 10-year baseline risk of a coronary event is 0.5%. A polygenic score places her in a stratum with 2.5× the average risk. Her 10-year absolute risk becomes:
options: 1.25%, an increase of 0.75 percentage points
2.5%, an increase of 2 percentage points
feedback: Correct — 2.5 × 0.5% = 1.25%, so the absolute increase is 0.75 percentage points. The relative risk sounds alarming; the decision-relevant quantity is that 0.75-point difference, which at her age rarely changes management.
2.5% would be the answer if the baseline were 1%. Multiply the actual baseline: 2.5 × 0.5% = 1.25%, an absolute rise of 0.75 points.
25% mistakes the multiplier for a percentage. A relative risk of 2.5 multiplies the baseline risk; it is not itself a risk.
The arithmetic slipped by a factor of ten: 0.5% × 2.5 = 1.25%, not 12.5%. Watch the decimal — this is exactly the slip that turns a rounding error into a scare.

questions.prompt: European-trained polygenic risk scores applied to individuals of African ancestry lose roughly how much predictive accuracy, per Martin et al. (2019)?
options: Essentially none — human genomes are 99.9% shared
About 1.2-fold lower
About 4.9-fold lower on average
They perform better, because African genomes carry more variation
feedback: Shared sequence is not the issue. What differs is allele frequency and linkage-disequilibrium structure, so the tag variants that proxy causal effects in one population stop proxying them in another.
Far too small. Martin et al. reported roughly 1.6-fold lower in Hispanic/Latino, 1.7-fold in South Asian and 2.5-fold in East Asian samples — and 4.9-fold lower in African ancestry.

Correct — an average 4.9-fold loss, driven by 79% of GWAS participants being of European descent. It is the largest equity problem in the field, and it makes current scores least useful in populations often carrying the heaviest cardiometabolic burden.
Greater African genetic diversity works against portability here, not for it: shorter linkage-disequilibrium blocks mean European-derived tag variants proxy the causal variants less well.

questions.prompt: Elliott et al. reported a C-statistic of 0.61 for a coronary polygenic score used alone. What does that number mean?
options: 61% of people with a high score develop coronary disease
Given one future case and one non-case, the score ranks the case higher 61% of the time
The score explains 61% of coronary disease risk
61% of the variants in the score are causal
feedback: The C-statistic is not an event rate. It is a ranking statistic and says nothing about the fraction of high scorers who go on to develop disease.

Correct — the C-statistic (equivalently the area under the ROC curve) is exactly this pairwise ranking probability. At 0.61 the score beats the 0.50 coin flip by a real but modest margin, and falls far short of the individual-level certainty marketing implies.
Variance explained and discrimination are different quantities. A C-statistic of 0.61 corresponds to a very modest share of variance on the liability scale, not 61% of it.
The C-statistic measures predictive discrimination, not the causal status of the variants. Most weighted variants in a modern score are tags, not causes.

questions.prompt: A patient is told he sits in the top 5% of the polygenic distribution for type 2 diabetes. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: He will almost certainly develop type 2 diabetes
His prior probability is shifted upward; most people in that stratum still never develop the disease, and nothing about his modifiable risk factors has changed
He can lower the score through diet and exercise
The result rules in a diagnosis and should trigger treatment
feedback: Even strong strata leave the majority unaffected. A polygenic score moves a distribution; it does not deliver an outcome to an individual.

Correct — a percentile is a shift in prior probability and nothing more. It also does not change what he can do: the score is fixed at conception while the absolute risk it estimates is substantially modifiable.
The score itself cannot change — it is a fixed function of his genotype. What diet and exercise change is the absolute risk, which is the number that actually matters.
A polygenic score is not diagnostic. It has no defined positive predictive value for an individual and does not on its own meet the standard for initiating treatment.

resources.label: NHGRI — Polygenic Risk Scores
resources.note: The federal genome institute's own explainer, and unusually candid: it states plainly that these scores measure relative rather than absolute risk and are most accurate in people of European ancestry.

resources.label: PGS Catalog — open database of published polygenic scores
resources.note: Every published score with its variant weights, development metadata and reported performance across ancestry groups. If a company quotes you a score, its ancestry-specific performance is probably listed here.

resources.label: Martin et al. (2019), "Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities," Nature Genetics
resources.note: The source of the 1.6× / 1.7× / 2.5× / 4.9× portability figures and the 79%-European participation statistic. Free full text; the figures are worth more than the prose.

concepts.title: Reading a Genetic Test: Bayes at the Bedside
concepts.summary: A genetic result is a likelihood ratio, not an answer — the same 'pathogenic variant detected' supports about a 33% lifetime cancer probability under population screening and about 72% in a family with a strong history, and a consumer-array 'negative' rules out almost nothing.

cards.h: Five tiers, one of which is not a result
cards.md:
Clinical laboratories classify variants on the five-tier scale set by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (**ACMG/AMP**; Richards et al., *Genetics in Medicine*, 2015):

**pathogenic · likely pathogenic · variant of uncertain significance (VUS) · likely benign · benign**

"Likely" is calibrated, not casual: it means the laboratory is at least **90%** confident. A **VUS** is neither a weak positive nor a mild warning. It is a **no-result** — the evidence is insufficient in either direction — and the guidelines are explicit that a VUS must not drive clinical action. Risk-reducing surgery performed on a VUS is a documented and entirely preventable harm.

What becomes of a VUS is quantifiable. Mersch et al. (*JAMA*, 2018) followed hereditary-cancer testing at one large laboratory from 2006 to 2016:

## 2,048 of 26,670 unique VUS were reclassified = 7.7%
## of those, 1,867 went to benign / likely benign = 91.2%

Only 8.7% were upgraded to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. Weighted by how many patients received each variant on a report, **24.9%** of all reported VUS were eventually reclassified; median time to an amended report was 1.17 years for downgrades. The base rate is unambiguous: a VUS on your report is roughly **ten times more likely** to end up benign than pathogenic.

**The ancestry bias.** Classification leans heavily on population frequency — a variant common among healthy people cannot be a high-penetrance cause of disease. Reference databases are overwhelmingly European, so a variant that is common and harmless in an under-sequenced population looks rare and therefore suspicious. Manrai et al. (*NEJM*, 2016) found several variants previously reported as pathogenic for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were significantly more common among Black Americans than white Americans and are in fact benign — patients and their relatives had been given genetic misdiagnoses. For the same structural reason, patients of non-European ancestry receive VUS results at substantially higher rates.

cards.h: ★ The same positive, two very different answers
cards.md:
A genetic result updates a prior. Work it in natural frequencies rather than formulas.

**Scenario A — population screening, no family history.** A woman receives a report of a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. Say the variant's carrier frequency in her population is 1 in 2,000 (0.05%), assay sensitivity is 99%, and the per-variant false-positive rate is 1 in 1,000 (specificity 99.9%). Among 100,000 women:

## carriers: 50 → true positives = 0.99 × 50 = 49.5
## non-carriers: 99,950 → false positives = 0.001 × 99,950 = 100.0
## PPV = 49.5 / (49.5 + 100.0) = 33%

Two of every three positives are wrong. Not hypothetical: Tandy-Connor et al. (*Genetics in Medicine*, 2018) found **40%** of variants flagged "increased risk" in direct-to-consumer raw data were false positives on clinical confirmation.

Now layer in **penetrance** — the probability a true carrier develops the disease. Kuchenbaecker et al. (*JAMA*, 2017; 9,856 carriers, prospective) put cumulative breast-cancer risk to age 80 at **72%** for BRCA1. Baseline United States female lifetime risk is about **13%**.

## P(cancer | positive) = 0.331×0.72 + 0.669×0.13 = 0.238 + 0.087 ≈ 33%

The number on the report is 72%. The number true of her is about **33%** — elevated, roughly 2.5× baseline, and less than half the headline.

**Scenario B — diagnostic, strong family history.** Same variant, same letter, but her mother and maternal aunt had breast cancer before 50, so a risk model puts her prior at 10%; and the laboratory sequenced the gene and confirmed the call by a second method (specificity 99.99%). Among 10,000 such women:

## carriers: 1,000 → 990 true positives; non-carriers: 9,000 → 0.9 false positives
## PPV = 990 / 990.9 = 99.9%  →  P(cancer) ≈ 0.999 × 0.72 ≈ 72%

Identical words on the page. **33% versus 72%** — decided entirely by the prior and the assay, not by the DNA.

cards.h: Arrays ask fixed questions; a negative may answer none of them
cards.md:
A consumer genotyping array is a fixed panel of probes. At each of several hundred thousand chosen positions it asks "is this letter an A or a G?" It cannot see a variant it has no probe for, and it does not read the rest of the gene at all. **Clinical sequencing** reads every base of the target genes, and adds deletion/duplication analysis for the large rearrangements that neither arrays nor plain sequencing detect.

The gap is enormous, and the numbers are public. 23andMe's FDA-authorised BRCA report covers **44** variants. More than **4,000** BRCA1/BRCA2 variants are known to raise cancer risk. The original 2018 authorisation covered **three** Ashkenazi founder variants, which account for roughly 87% of BRCA1 and 93% of BRCA2 pathogenic variants in Ashkenazi Jewish people — and a small minority of them in everyone else.

So read a consumer "variants not detected" result for what it literally is:

## P(none of the 44 tested variants), NOT P(no pathogenic BRCA variant)

In odds terms the negative likelihood ratio for a non-Ashkenazi woman is close to **1** — the result barely moves her prior at all. A woman with three relatives who had early breast cancer, who reads a consumer-array "negative" and skips clinical testing, has been actively harmed by a technically correct report. The FDA authorisation letter states this limitation in writing; almost nobody reads it.

Two further distinctions worth carrying:

- A **true negative** means the family's specific, already-identified pathogenic variant was tested for and is absent. That is genuinely reassuring.
- An **uninformative negative** means no pathogenic variant was found in a family where none was ever identified. That is not reassurance; it is the absence of information.

The practical rule runs in both directions: **never act on a consumer-array positive without clinical confirmation, and never take reassurance from a consumer-array negative.**

questions.prompt: Screen 100,000 women for a variant carried by 1 in 2,000, using an assay with 99% sensitivity and a 1-in-1,000 false-positive rate. What is the positive predictive value of a positive result?
options: About 99%
About 33%
About 50%
About 5%
feedback: 99% is the sensitivity, not the positive predictive value. Sensitivity asks P(positive | carrier); PPV asks P(carrier | positive). With a rare variant those two quantities diverge dramatically.

Correct — 50 carriers give 49.5 true positives, while 99,950 non-carriers at a 0.1% error rate give 100 false positives. PPV = 49.5/149.5 ≈ 33%. When the prior is tiny, even a very specific assay produces more false positives than true ones.
50% would require true and false positives to be equal. Here the false positives (100) outnumber the true positives (49.5) by about two to one, pulling the answer below half.
5% understates it. The assay is genuinely informative — it lifts the probability from 0.05% to about 33%, a roughly 660-fold update. It just is not the near-certainty the report implies.

questions.prompt: A report returns a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in BRCA2. What is the appropriate reading?
options: A weak positive — begin enhanced surveillance on the basis of the variant
A no-result that must not drive clinical action; if it is ever reclassified, roughly 9 times in 10 it is downgraded to benign
Proof that the gene is normal
Sufficient grounds to consider risk-reducing surgery
feedback: A VUS is not a graded positive. The evidence is insufficient in both directions, and treating it as a weak positive imports risk and anxiety that the data do not support.

Correct — ACMG/AMP guidance is that a VUS must not be used for clinical decisions, and Mersch et al. found that among reclassified VUS 91.2% were downgraded to benign or likely benign versus 8.7% upgraded. The base rate strongly favours benign.
A VUS is not a normal result either. It is the explicit absence of a conclusion: the laboratory found something it cannot classify in either direction.
This is the documented harm case. Risk-reducing surgery has been performed on the basis of a VUS, and preventing exactly that is why the classification tier exists.

questions.prompt: A woman of Northern European ancestry with three first-degree relatives who developed breast cancer before 50 receives a consumer-array report reading 'BRCA variants not detected.' What should she conclude?
options: Her BRCA risk is ruled out
Essentially nothing — the array tests 44 of more than 4,000 known pathogenic variants, so the negative likelihood ratio is near 1 and clinical sequencing is still indicated
Her family history must be coincidental
The array is defective and the test should be repeated
feedback: This is the dangerous misreading the concept exists to prevent. The array answered a far narrower question than the one she is actually asking.

Correct — the result is P(none of the 44 tested variants), not P(no pathogenic BRCA variant). Her prior is high on family history, and a test that barely shifts the odds leaves it high. Clinical sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis is the correct next step.
An early-onset pattern across three first-degree relatives is far from coincidental, and in any case the test performed cannot speak to it in either direction.
The array worked exactly as designed. The failure is interpretive: a small fixed panel of probes cannot deliver an informative negative for a gene with thousands of pathogenic variants.

questions.prompt: Why does the identical laboratory sentence — 'pathogenic BRCA1 variant detected' — support about a 33% lifetime breast-cancer probability in one woman and about 72% in another?
options: Because the penetrance of the variant differs between the two women
Because the pre-test probability and the assay's error rate differ, changing the probability that the call is a true positive
Because one of the two reports is simply wrong
Because lifetime risk in carriers is not really knowable
feedback: The variant and its 72% penetrance are the same in both scenarios. What differs is the probability that she actually carries it — about 33% under screening, 99.9% in the diagnostic setting.

Correct — this is Bayes. Under screening (prior 1 in 2,000, array-class error rate) the positive predictive value is only about 33%, so expected risk is 0.33×72% + 0.67×13% ≈ 33%. With a strong family history and a confirmed sequencing call the PPV is 99.9% and the answer collapses to the penetrance itself.
Neither report is wrong. Both correctly state what was observed; the difference lies entirely in what that observation implies given the prior.
Carrier lifetime risk is well characterised — Kuchenbaecker et al. measured 72% cumulative breast-cancer risk to age 80 for BRCA1 carriers in a prospective cohort of 9,856 women.

resources.label: ClinVar — NCBI's public archive of variant–phenotype interpretations
resources.note: Look up any variant on your report and see how many laboratories classified it, whether they agreed, and when the classification last changed — the single most useful reality check on a genetic result.

resources.label: Mersch et al. (2018), "Prevalence of Variant Reclassification Following Hereditary Cancer Genetic Testing," JAMA
resources.note: Source of the 7.7% / 24.9% reclassification rates and the 91.2%-downgraded figure. The base rates that should govern how anyone reacts to a VUS.

resources.label: Manrai et al. (2016), "Genetic Misdiagnoses and the Potential for Health Disparities," NEJM
resources.note: The concrete case: benign variants common in Black Americans were reported as causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because control databases were European. The mechanism behind ancestry-skewed VUS rates, in one study.

concepts.title: Pharmacogenomics — the genetics that changes a prescription today
concepts.summary: A handful of gene–drug pairs already carry enough evidence to change the dose or the drug at the bedside, and the direction of the effect flips depending on whether the enzyme clears the drug or activates it.

cards.h: What pharmacogenomics is — star alleles and the metaboliser ladder
cards.md:
**Pharmacogenomics (PGx)** is the study of how inherited variation changes drug response. It is not polygenic risk scoring: the clinically useful signals are a small number of **large-effect variants in single genes** — drug-metabolising enzymes (the **cytochrome P450** family, written *CYP*), membrane transporters, and immune **HLA** (human leukocyte antigen) types.

Variants are named as **star alleles**. `CYP2C19*1` is the reference ("normal function"), `*2` and `*3` are **loss-of-function (LOF)**, `*17` is increased-function. Your two inherited alleles form a **diplotype**; each allele carries an activity value, and the sum maps onto a **metaboliser phenotype**:

- **Poor metaboliser (PM)** — two no-function alleles; essentially no enzyme activity.
- **Intermediate (IM)** — one no-function allele, or two reduced-function ones.
- **Normal (NM)** — the reference state (older papers call this "extensive").
- **Rapid / Ultrarapid (RM/UM)** — increased-function alleles, or an outright duplication of the gene.

This ladder is the unit of clinical action: a laboratory reports a diplotype, and a guideline acts on the phenotype. Note what is *not* being measured. The assay reads DNA, not enzyme activity, so the phenotype it assigns is a prediction — a good one for the well-characterised alleles, and a blank for the rare or novel ones the panel was never designed to call.

cards.h: Why the effect flips direction — plus CPIC and phenoconversion
cards.md:
**The direction of the clinical effect flips depending on the drug.** For an *active* drug cleared by the enzyme, a poor metaboliser accumulates drug and gets toxicity. For a **prodrug** the enzyme must *activate*, a poor metaboliser makes too little active compound and gets treatment failure.

Codeine is the clean illustration. **CYP2D6** converts codeine to morphine, so poor metabolisers get no analgesia at all, while **ultrarapid** metabolisers generate a morphine spike — which is why the FDA carries a boxed warning against codeine in children and contraindicates it after tonsillectomy. Same gene, same drug, opposite ends of the ladder, opposite harms.

The rules for acting on a result come from **CPIC** — the **Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium** (now part of **ClinPGx**, which merged CPIC, PharmGKB and PharmCAT into one resource in 2025). Read its remit precisely: CPIC deliberately does *not* tell you whether to order a test. It tells you what to do with a genotype **you already have**. That distinction is the entire pre-emptive-testing argument, and it returns in the companion lesson.

One trap breaks the whole model: **phenoconversion**. A genotypic normal metaboliser co-prescribed a strong enzyme inhibitor behaves like a poor metaboliser — a patient on fluoxetine or paroxetine, both potent CYP2D6 inhibitors, is functionally CYP2D6-deficient no matter what the genotype says. Genotype is fixed for life; phenotype is genotype *plus* the current medication list, and it changes every time that list does.

cards.h: CYP2C19 and clopidogrel — certain mechanism, uncertain benefit
cards.md:
**CYP2C19 → clopidogrel.** Clopidogrel (Plavix) is a **prodrug**; CYP2C19 performs the activating oxidation. Poor and intermediate metabolisers form less active thiol metabolite, achieve less platelet inhibition, and suffer more stent thrombosis after **PCI** (percutaneous coronary intervention). The FDA added a **boxed warning** in 2010; CPIC recommends prasugrel or ticagrelor instead for PM/IM patients with **ACS** (acute coronary syndrome) or undergoing PCI.

LOF alleles are common and unevenly distributed by ancestry: poor metabolisers run on the order of 2% of Europeans but well over 10% of East Asians. That single fact is why a genotype-blind default of "everyone gets clopidogrel" fails differently in different populations.

Now the honest part — what the outcome trials actually showed. **TAILOR-PCI** (2020) found roughly a one-third relative reduction in ischaemic events under genotype guidance but *narrowly missed statistical significance*. **POPular Genetics** showed genotype-guided de-escalation was non-inferior for thrombotic events while producing **less bleeding**. The pharmacological mechanism is not in doubt; the magnitude of the outcome benefit — and therefore whether routine testing pays for itself — still is.

cards.h: Warfarin and simvastatin — the biggest effect size, and the transporter
cards.md:
**CYP2C9 + VKORC1 → warfarin.** *VKORC1* encodes warfarin's actual **target**, vitamin K epoxide reductase — not an enzyme that metabolises it. Its −1639G>A promoter variant lowers expression of the target, so less drug is needed to inhibit it. *CYP2C9\*2* and *\*3* act on the other side of the problem, slowing clearance of the potent S-enantiomer. Combined with age, body size and interacting drugs, genotype explains roughly **half** of the between-patient dose variance — the largest effect size in all of pharmacogenomics.

Which makes the trial record instructive: **COAG** (2013) was negative, **EU-PACT** positive, **GIFT** (2017) positive on a composite endpoint. A large, well-replicated pharmacological effect did not translate cleanly into better outcomes, partly because attentive INR monitoring already corrects the dose empirically within days. And **DOACs** (direct oral anticoagulants) have since taken most of warfarin's indications, shrinking the practical footprint of the whole question.

**SLCO1B1 → simvastatin.** *SLCO1B1* encodes **OATP1B1**, the hepatic uptake transporter that pulls statins out of portal blood into liver cells. The `c.521T>C` (*\*5*) variant reduces uptake, so more drug stays in the systemic circulation and reaches muscle. The **SEARCH** genome-wide study (2008) found an odds ratio near **4.5 per copy** for myopathy on simvastatin 80 mg, with the majority of cases in that trial attributable to the variant. CPIC's guidance is drug- and dose-specific — strong for simvastatin, weaker for atorvastatin, minimal for fluvastatin — so the action is usually "pick a different statin", not "abandon statins". The FDA separately restricted the 80 mg simvastatin dose in 2011.

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old is undergoing PCI for acute coronary syndrome. Pre-emptive genotyping returns CYP2C19 *2/*2 (poor metaboliser). What does CPIC guidance support?
options: Use prasugrel or ticagrelor instead of clopidogrel
Prescribe clopidogrel at double the usual maintenance dose
Switch the antiplatelet to warfarin
Proceed with standard clopidogrel — genotype affects only bleeding risk
feedback: Correct — clopidogrel is a prodrug that CYP2C19 must activate, so a poor metaboliser gets inadequate platelet inhibition; CPIC recommends an alternative agent that does not depend on CYP2C19.
No — dose escalation was tested and does not reliably overcome a *2/*2 genotype; the activating enzyme is essentially absent, so more prodrug does not fix it.
No — warfarin is an anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet agent, and does not substitute for P2Y12 inhibition after stenting.
No — the direction is the opposite: poor metabolisers get too LITTLE active drug, and the documented harm is stent thrombosis, not bleeding.

questions.prompt: Why is a CYP2D6 ULTRARAPID metaboliser at risk from codeine, when for most drugs the risk sits with poor metabolisers?
options: Codeine is a prodrug — CYP2D6 converts it to morphine, so extra enzyme produces a morphine surge
Ultrarapid metabolisers cannot clear codeine, so it accumulates
Codeine is toxic only in its unmetabolised form
Ultrarapid metabolisers have an allergic reaction to codeine
feedback: Correct — for a prodrug the direction flips: more enzyme means more ACTIVE drug. This drove the FDA boxed warning and the contraindication in children after tonsillectomy.
No — ultrarapid means faster conversion, not impaired clearance; the problem is too much morphine, not retained codeine.
No — codeine itself is a weak opioid; the risk comes from the morphine it is converted into.
No — this is a dose-related pharmacological effect on respiration, not an immune hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.prompt: A patient genotyped as a CYP2D6 normal metaboliser has been taking paroxetine, a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor, for two years. How should you interpret their CYP2D6 phenotype for a new prescription?
options: Functionally poor — this is phenoconversion, and the drug list overrides the genotype
Normal — genotype is fixed, so the phenotype cannot change
Ultrarapid — inhibitors upregulate the enzyme over time
Indeterminate — CYP2D6 genotype has no clinical meaning
feedback: Correct — a strong inhibitor converts a genotypic normal metaboliser into a functional poor metaboliser. Phenotype is genotype plus the current medication list, and it changes whenever that list does.
No — the genotype is indeed fixed, but the phenotype it predicts is not. Enzyme inhibition is exactly the case where the prediction fails.
No — inhibitors reduce activity. Enzyme induction, by rifampin for example, is a separate phenomenon and does not apply to paroxetine on CYP2D6.
No — CYP2D6 genotype is clinically meaningful for codeine, tamoxifen and several antidepressants; the point here is that co-medication modifies its interpretation.

questions.prompt: A patient develops myopathy on simvastatin 80 mg and is found to carry SLCO1B1 c.521T>C. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Switch to a statin less dependent on OATP1B1 uptake, or use a lower-intensity alternative
Stop all statins permanently — the variant contraindicates the whole class
Continue simvastatin 80 mg with monthly creatine kinase monitoring
Increase the simvastatin dose to overcome reduced hepatic uptake
feedback: Correct — CPIC's statin guidance is drug- and dose-specific. The effect is strongest for simvastatin and minimal for fluvastatin, so the action is usually to change statin rather than to abandon the class.
No — that forfeits a proven cardiovascular benefit. The variant modifies risk for particular statins at particular doses, not for lipid-lowering as a whole.
No — the FDA restricted the 80 mg simvastatin dose in 2011, and continuing the offending drug and dose after a myopathy event is the one option clearly to avoid.
No — reduced hepatic uptake means MORE drug in the systemic circulation reaching muscle, not less drug at the target. Raising the dose worsens the exposure that caused the problem.

questions.prompt: VKORC1 variants affect warfarin dosing by a different mechanism from CYP2C9 variants. What is the difference?
options: VKORC1 encodes warfarin's target enzyme, so the variant changes how much target there is to inhibit; CYP2C9 variants change how fast warfarin is cleared
VKORC1 is a transporter and CYP2C9 is a receptor
VKORC1 affects absorption from the gut; CYP2C9 affects renal excretion
They act by the same mechanism — both are metabolising enzymes
feedback: Correct — this is a pharmacodynamic versus pharmacokinetic distinction. VKORC1 is vitamin K epoxide reductase, the drug target itself, and its promoter variant lowers target expression, so less warfarin is needed.
No — VKORC1 is an enzyme and is the drug's target, not a transporter; CYP2C9 is a metabolising enzyme, not a receptor.
No — neither gene acts on absorption or renal excretion; warfarin is well absorbed and cleared hepatically.
No — only CYP2C9 is a metabolising enzyme. Treating them as equivalent hides the reason genotype explains so much dose variance: the two genes act on opposite sides of the dose–response relationship.

resources.label: CPIC gene–drug guidelines (ClinPGx)
resources.note: The primary source: peer-reviewed, per-pair dosing recommendations with strength-of-evidence ratings. CPIC, PharmGKB and PharmCAT merged into ClinPGx in 2025, so older cpicpgx.org and pharmgkb.org links now redirect here.

resources.label: FDA — Table of Pharmacogenetic Associations
resources.note: FDA's own list of associations it considers sufficiently supported, split by whether the evidence bears on drug levels, on efficacy, or on adverse events. Note FDA's explicit caveat: inclusion does not mean FDA recommends testing before prescribing.

concepts.title: Pharmacogenomics II — the tests that exist to prevent a catastrophe
concepts.summary: DPYD, HLA-B*57:01 and TPMT/NUDT15 are the pairs where a genotype prevents a life-threatening reaction rather than fine-tuning a dose — and they are also where the field's ancestry gap and its evidence limits show most clearly.

cards.h: DPYD and the fluoropyrimidines — when a standard dose is an overdose
cards.md:
**DPYD → fluoropyrimidines.** **DPD** (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) catabolises well over 80% of a dose of **5-fluorouracil (5-FU)** or capecitabine. If DPD is missing, a standard dose behaves like a massive overdose.

Four well-characterised *DPYD* variants (\*2A, c.2846A>T, c.1236G>A/HapB3, \*13) cause severe — sometimes fatal — mucositis, diarrhoea and myelosuppression. CPIC assigns a **gene activity score** from 0 to 2 and acts on it directly: halve the starting dose at an activity score of 1–1.5, avoid the drug entirely at 0, then titrate upward if the patient tolerates it. Roughly 3–8% of people of European ancestry carry a reduced-function allele; complete deficiency is rare.

This is also the clearest example of regulators diverging on the *same* evidence. The **EMA** (European Medicines Agency) has recommended pre-treatment DPD testing since 2020 and the UK NHS made it routine; US adoption has been slower and remains uneven institution by institution. If you need the current US position, read the current label rather than a textbook — this one has been moving.

cards.h: HLA-B*57:01 and abacavir — the pair that became standard of care
cards.md:
**HLA-B\*57:01 → abacavir.** This is the case where testing did not merely get recommended — it *became* the standard of care, and the pair is now the field's proof of concept.

Carriers of the **HLA-B\*57:01** allele develop a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction to the HIV drug abacavir. The mechanism is immunological rather than metabolic: the drug alters the peptide-binding groove of that specific HLA molecule, so the immune system sees self-peptides as foreign. The prospective **PREDICT-1** trial (2008) drove immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity to **zero** by screening before the first dose — a negative predictive value of essentially 100%. Testing is in the label and is done universally.

Three features made this pair uniquely tractable, and they explain why most gene–drug pairs never get here: the outcome is severe and unambiguous, the allele is a near-perfect predictor rather than a modest risk factor, and an equally good alternative drug exists. When all three hold, universal screening is easy to justify.

Same logic, different allele: **HLA-B\*15:02** and carbamazepine-induced **Stevens–Johnson syndrome** in patients of Southeast Asian ancestry, where the FDA label recommends testing before starting the drug.

cards.h: TPMT, NUDT15, and the ancestry gap in every panel
cards.md:
**TPMT and NUDT15 → thiopurines.** Azathioprine, mercaptopurine and thioguanine — used in inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disease and childhood leukaemia — are inactivated by **thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT)**. A poor metaboliser given a standard dose can develop life-threatening myelosuppression, so CPIC recommends starting at a small fraction of the usual dose or choosing another agent.

Then comes the part that should change how you read every pharmacogenomic panel. **NUDT15** (nudix hydrolase 15) was identified only in **2014**, and it matters enormously: *TPMT* variants are rare in East Asian and Hispanic populations, while *NUDT15* variants are not. A panel built on European data therefore under-protects exactly the patients who most need protecting, and it does so silently — the result comes back "normal".

This is the field's central equity problem stated in a single gene pair. Reference allele frequencies, variant classifications and even the star-allele definitions were derived largely from European cohorts. When a panel returns a reassuring result for a patient whose ancestry is poorly represented in those cohorts, the correct reading is *"no known variant was found on this panel"* — not *"this patient has normal enzyme function"*.

cards.h: Where the evidence actually stops
cards.md:
**Where the evidence actually stops.** Acting on a genotype you already have is well supported. **Pre-emptive panel testing of everyone**, before any drug is prescribed, is a different claim and is not settled.

The strongest evidence for it is **PREPARE** (2023), a roughly 7,000-patient European study of a 12-gene panel that reported about a **30% reduction in clinically relevant adverse drug reactions**. That is a real and important result. It is also open-label, with outcome ascertainment that depends partly on subjective reporting, and no trial has demonstrated a mortality benefit.

The remaining objections are practical rather than biological:

- **Cost-effectiveness depends on the drug mix.** A panel pays for itself in a population that will actually receive clopidogrel, thiopurines or fluoropyrimidines; much less so otherwise.
- **US reimbursement is patchy**, and coverage decisions differ by payer and by pair.
- **A result nobody sees does nothing.** Without hard-wired clinical decision support firing at the moment of prescribing, a genotype filed in a chart years earlier is invisible.
- **Panels age.** Alleles get reclassified, and *NUDT15* is the standing reminder that the relevant gene may not have been discovered yet.

Reasonable clinicians disagree about pre-emptive panels. Nobody serious disagrees about DPYD before a fluoropyrimidine or HLA-B\*57:01 before abacavir. Hold those two claims apart — anyone selling certainty across the whole field is overselling.

questions.prompt: A patient is due to start capecitabine. DPYD genotyping returns an activity score of 1. What does CPIC guidance support?
options: Start at roughly half the standard dose and titrate upward if tolerated
Give the standard dose and monitor closely for mucositis
Avoid fluoropyrimidines entirely
Increase the dose, since reduced DPD means less drug reaches the tumour
feedback: Correct — an activity score of 1 or 1.5 indicates an intermediate metaboliser: halve the starting dose, then titrate upward guided by toxicity. Complete avoidance is reserved for an activity score of 0.
No — 5-FU toxicity in a DPD-deficient patient can be fatal and can develop faster than monitoring catches it. The dose reduction is the intervention.
No — that is the recommendation for an activity score of 0. An intermediate metaboliser can usually receive the drug safely at a reduced starting dose.
No — DPD catabolises the drug, so less DPD means higher systemic exposure, not lower. Raising the dose is precisely the fatal error this test exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: For which gene–drug pair has pre-treatment testing become genuinely universal standard of care, backed by a prospective trial that drove confirmed reactions to zero?
options: HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir
CYP2C9 before warfarin
SLCO1B1 before simvastatin
CYP2C19 before every proton pump inhibitor
feedback: Correct — PREDICT-1 (2008) showed screening eliminated immunologically confirmed abacavir hypersensitivity; testing is in the label and is done everywhere.
No — warfarin genotyping has the biggest effect on dose variance but the outcome trials conflicted (COAG negative, EU-PACT and GIFT positive), so it never became universal.
No — SLCO1B1 guidance is real but is used to pick a statin and a dose, not as a mandatory pre-prescription screen.
No — CYP2C19 affects PPI exposure, but that is an efficacy-tuning question rather than a safety screen, and it is not routine practice.

questions.prompt: Three features made HLA-B*57:01 screening easy to justify where most gene–drug pairs fail. Which set is correct?
options: A severe unambiguous outcome, an allele that is a near-perfect predictor, and an equally good alternative drug
A common allele, a cheap assay, and a drug with no alternative
A mild reversible outcome, a rare allele, and strong patient demand
A metabolic mechanism, a dose-dependent effect, and a wide therapeutic index
feedback: Correct — when the harm is severe and unmistakable, the test is close to deterministic rather than probabilistic, and switching costs the patient nothing therapeutically, universal screening follows almost automatically.
No — having no alternative drug undercuts the case for screening, because a positive result would leave you with nothing useful to do about it.
No — a mild reversible outcome is exactly the situation where pre-treatment screening is hard to justify clinically or economically.
No — the abacavir reaction is immunological, not metabolic, and it is not dose-dependent. A wide therapeutic index would argue against needing a test at all.

questions.prompt: A patient of Korean ancestry has a normal TPMT result but develops profound myelosuppression on azathioprine. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A NUDT15 loss-of-function variant — common in East Asian populations and absent from TPMT-only testing
The TPMT assay is unreliable in people of East Asian ancestry
Azathioprine has no genetic determinants of toxicity beyond TPMT
Poor metaboliser status for CYP2C19
feedback: Correct — NUDT15, identified in 2014, is the dominant thiopurine toxicity gene in East Asian and Hispanic populations, where TPMT variants are rare. A European-derived panel systematically under-protects these patients.
No — the TPMT assay works fine; the problem is that the relevant variant is in a different gene the panel never looked at.
No — NUDT15 is a second, independently established determinant, now in the FDA labelling alongside TPMT.
No — CYP2C19 has no established role in thiopurine metabolism; it matters for clopidogrel, PPIs and some antidepressants.

questions.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the state of evidence for pre-emptive multi-gene pharmacogenomic panel testing in everyone?
options: One large open-label study (PREPARE, 2023) reported roughly a 30% reduction in clinically relevant adverse drug reactions, but no trial has shown a mortality benefit and cost-effectiveness remains contested
Randomised trials have established a clear survival benefit, and panels are now standard of care
There is no evidence of any benefit, and no professional body supports pre-emptive testing
It is settled science — CPIC guidelines instruct clinicians to genotype every patient before prescribing
feedback: Correct — the signal is real but the study was open-label with subjective ADR ascertainment; honest practice is to describe both the finding and its limits.
No — no trial has demonstrated a survival benefit, and pre-emptive panels are not standard of care in most health systems.
No — that overstates the negative case; PREPARE reported a meaningful reduction in adverse reactions and several health systems run pre-emptive programmes.
No — CPIC deliberately does NOT tell clinicians whom to test. It states what to do with a genotype you already have.

questions.prompt: A pharmacogenomic panel returns 'no variants detected' for a patient whose ancestry is poorly represented in the reference databases. What is the correct reading?
options: No known variant was found on this panel — which is a weaker claim than 'enzyme function is normal'
Enzyme function is confirmed normal, so standard dosing is safe
The result is invalid and the test should be repeated
The patient almost certainly carries an undetected variant
feedback: Correct — a panel can only report what it interrogates. Allele definitions and frequency data were derived largely from European cohorts, so a negative result carries less information in an under-represented population.
No — this is the specific inference the NUDT15 story warns against. 'Not found' and 'not present' are different claims, and conflating them is how patients get hurt.
No — the assay performed correctly. The limitation is in panel content and reference data, not in the run.
No — that overcorrects. Most such patients have no relevant variant; the point is calibrated uncertainty, not assumed positivity.

resources.label: FDA — Table of Pharmacogenomic Biomarkers in Drug Labeling
resources.note: The authoritative answer to 'is this actually on the label?' — including the clopidogrel boxed warning and the TPMT/NUDT15 and DPYD entries. Check here before quoting any regulatory claim, because the labels move.

resources.label: ClinPGx — pharmacogenomic knowledge base (formerly PharmGKB)
resources.note: Variant-level annotations, allele frequencies by population, and clinical annotation levels of evidence. The population-frequency tables are the fastest way to check whether a panel is likely to be informative for a given patient's ancestry.

concepts.title: Cancer Genetics I — germline predisposition and the question it answers
concepts.summary: A germline test asks who else in the family is at risk; Knudson's two-hit model explains why carriers present earlier, and BRCA and Lynch show why the answer is a gene-specific range rather than a single number.

cards.h: Two words, two different questions
cards.md:
Two words do most of the work in cancer genetics, and conflating them causes real harm.

- **Germline** variants are inherited. They are present in every nucleated cell from conception, they can be passed to children, and they are detected from **blood or saliva**.
- **Somatic** mutations are acquired during life inside a cell lineage. They are present only in the tumour and its descendants, they are **not heritable**, and they are detected by sequencing **tumour tissue** or tumour DNA shed into plasma.

Hold onto the practical consequence, because it decides which test you order:

- A **germline** test answers *"who else in this family is at risk, and what surveillance or risk-reducing surgery does this person need?"*
- A **tumour** test answers *"what drug might work against this cancer right now?"*

Two cautions about the sample itself. In a patient with leukaemia, a "germline" blood sample is contaminated with tumour, so skin fibroblasts or buccal cells are used instead. And a few percent of **tumour-only** panels turn up a variant that is in fact germline — a finding that obliges a confirmatory germline test and genetic counselling, not a shrug. Allele fraction is the usual clue: a germline variant sits near 50% (or 100%) in every tissue, while a somatic one sits wherever the tumour clone puts it.

cards.h: Knudson's two hits — a model derived from arithmetic
cards.md:
**Knudson's two-hit model (1971)** explains why inherited predisposition behaves the way it does — and it was derived from arithmetic, not from a sequencer.

Alfred Knudson analysed the age-of-onset distribution of retinoblastoma and saw that hereditary cases appeared earlier and were frequently **bilateral and multifocal**, while sporadic cases appeared later and singly. The sporadic curve fitted a two-event process; the hereditary curve fitted a one-event process. His inference: a **tumour suppressor gene** needs *both* copies knocked out to release the brake. A germline carrier is born with the first hit already present in every retinal cell, so only one further somatic event is needed — near-certain across millions of cells. A non-carrier needs two independent hits in the same cell, which is rare. *RB1* was cloned years later and proved him right.

Two refinements matter in practice:

- The two-hit rule applies to **tumour suppressors** — *RB1*, *TP53*, *BRCA1/2*, the mismatch repair genes. **Oncogenes** such as *KRAS*, *BRAF* and *EGFR* are gain-of-function and act dominantly at the cellular level: one hit is enough.
- "The second hit" is often not a point mutation at all, but **loss of heterozygosity**, promoter methylation, or a structural deletion. This is why a panel looking only for point mutations can miss the second event entirely.

cards.h: BRCA1 and BRCA2 — why the numbers are ranges
cards.md:
**BRCA1 and BRCA2** are the canonical example, and the numbers deserve care. The NCI currently states that **more than 60%** of women carrying a harmful *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* variant develop breast cancer in their lifetime, against about **13%** in the general population. Ovarian risk splits by gene: about **39–58%** for *BRCA1* and **13–29%** for *BRCA2*, against roughly **1.1%** at baseline. Large prospective cohort studies published in 2017 put cumulative breast cancer risk to age 80 near **72%** for *BRCA1* and **69%** for *BRCA2*.

The ranges are real biology, not sloppiness. **Penetrance is modified** by family history burden, by common polygenic background, and by where the variant sits in the gene. The same pathogenic variant carries materially different risk in a family with many early cancers than in one with none — which is part of why prospective estimates from ascertained cohorts run higher than population-level figures. Quoting a single percentage to a patient overstates the precision of what is actually known.

Two further points. *BRCA2* raises male breast and prostate cancer risk, and both genes raise pancreatic risk — so "the breast/ovarian genes" undersells them. And germline *BRCA* status is now also a **treatment** biomarker: PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality in homologous-recombination-deficient tumours. The clean germline-versus-somatic division of labour therefore blurs at the edges. A germline test can, these days, change the drug too.

cards.h: Lynch syndrome, and why family history still counts
cards.md:
**Lynch syndrome** arises from germline variants in the **mismatch repair (MMR)** genes *MLH1*, *MSH2*, *MSH6* and *PMS2*, or from *EPCAM* deletions that silence *MSH2*. Losing MMR produces **microsatellite instability (MSI)** — slippage in short repeat tracts that the repair machinery would normally correct.

It is the commonest inherited colorectal cancer syndrome, and in women **endometrial cancer is often the sentinel cancer**, appearing first. Risk is strongly **gene-specific**: colorectal risk to age 70 runs roughly 40–50% for *MLH1* and *MSH2*, but is substantially lower for *MSH6* and *PMS2* (on the order of 10–20%). Manage per gene, not per syndrome — a *PMS2* carrier and an *MLH1* carrier do not need the same colonoscopy interval.

Lynch is also where somatic testing points *back* to the germline. **Universal reflex screening** of colorectal and endometrial tumours by MMR immunohistochemistry or MSI testing is standard, with *BRAF* V600E or *MLH1* promoter methylation used to separate sporadic MLH1 loss (common, age-related, not inherited) from true Lynch.

**Why family history still counts.** A negative panel is not an all-clear. Most strong family clusters remain genetically unexplained, panels miss deep intronic and structural variants, and **variants of uncertain significance (VUS)** are reported far more often in people of non-European ancestry because the reference databases are skewed — the same equity problem that shows up in pharmacogenomics. A striking pedigree justifies intensified surveillance whether or not a gene is found. The pedigree is data.

questions.prompt: A 44-year-old woman has triple-negative breast cancer; her mother and maternal aunt had ovarian cancer. Her oncologist has already sent the tumour for a somatic panel. Her sister asks whether she should be screened. Which test answers the sister's question?
options: A germline test on the patient's blood or saliva
The tumour panel already sent — it will report any BRCA variant
A liquid biopsy for circulating tumour DNA
Repeat mammography on the sister; genetic testing adds nothing
feedback: Correct — only a germline test on non-tumour DNA establishes an inherited, heritable variant. That is the result the sister can be tested for, and it drives her surveillance and risk-reducing options.

No — a tumour panel reports mutations present in the cancer, which may be somatic-only. Without a matched normal sample it cannot separate inherited from acquired, so it cannot answer a family-risk question.
No — ctDNA is tumour-derived by definition. It is a treatment-selection and disease-monitoring tool, not a heritability test.
No — this pedigree (early-onset triple-negative breast cancer plus two ovarian cancers) is a textbook indication for germline testing, and the result changes management for the whole family.

questions.prompt: Under Knudson's two-hit model, why does hereditary retinoblastoma present earlier and more often bilaterally than the sporadic form?
options: The carrier is born with one hit already present in every retinal cell, so only one further somatic event is needed
The inherited mutation is more damaging than an acquired one
Hereditary tumours grow faster because they arise in younger tissue
Carriers inherit an oncogene that is active from birth
feedback: Correct — one germline hit plus one somatic hit is far likelier, across millions of cells, than two independent somatic hits in the same cell. That is exactly what Knudson inferred from the age-of-onset curves in 1971.
No — the variants are often identical; what differs is that the carrier starts one step further along in every single cell.
No — growth rate is not the mechanism. The model is about the probability of accumulating the required number of hits.
No — RB1 is a tumour suppressor requiring loss of both copies. Oncogenes act dominantly with a single gain-of-function hit and follow different logic.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to tell a BRCA1 carrier that her lifetime breast cancer risk is a single fixed percentage?
options: Penetrance is modified by family history burden, polygenic background and variant position, so the same variant carries different risk in different families
Because the published estimates are known to be fabricated
Because BRCA1 is not actually associated with breast cancer risk
Because risk cannot be estimated at all without whole-genome sequencing
feedback: Correct — this is why published figures appear as ranges, and why estimates from ascertained prospective cohorts run higher than population-level ones. A single number implies precision the evidence does not support.
No — the estimates are sound; the issue is that penetrance genuinely varies between families, not that the data are unreliable.
No — the association is among the best established in cancer genetics. The uncertainty concerns magnitude in an individual, not existence.
No — useful risk estimation is routine from a targeted test plus a pedigree. Whole-genome sequencing is not required and would not resolve the modifier problem.

questions.prompt: A colorectal tumour shows loss of MLH1 protein on immunohistochemistry. What is the appropriate next step before concluding the patient has Lynch syndrome?
options: Test for MLH1 promoter methylation or BRAF V600E, which indicate sporadic rather than inherited MLH1 loss
Proceed straight to risk-reducing colectomy
Conclude Lynch syndrome and test all first-degree relatives immediately
Repeat the immunohistochemistry on a second tissue block
feedback: Correct — sporadic MLH1 loss from age-related promoter hypermethylation is far commoner than Lynch syndrome, and BRAF V600E points the same way. This reflex step is why universal tumour screening works without flooding genetics clinics.
No — surgery cannot be justified before the germline question is resolved, and MLH1 loss alone does not establish an inherited syndrome.
No — cascade testing of relatives on an unconfirmed result generates substantial unnecessary anxiety and cost; most MLH1-deficient tumours are sporadic.
No — the immunohistochemistry result is not in doubt. The question is what caused the loss, which requires a different assay.

questions.prompt: A patient with a striking family history of early colorectal cancer has a negative multi-gene panel. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Intensified surveillance is still warranted — most strong family clusters remain genetically unexplained
The family history can now be disregarded and standard screening applies
The panel result proves the cancers were environmental in origin
The patient should be retested annually until a variant appears
feedback: Correct — panels miss deep intronic and structural variants, polygenic contributions are not captured, and much heritability remains unaccounted for. The pedigree is data in its own right and should drive management.
No — this is the most consequential misreading of a negative panel. Empiric family-history-based screening exists precisely for this situation.
No — a negative panel tests only the genes on the panel. It says nothing about whether an unmeasured genetic factor is present.
No — annual retesting is not useful. Periodic reanalysis as panels and variant classifications are updated is reasonable; yearly repeat testing is not.

resources.label: NCI — BRCA gene changes: cancer risk and genetic testing
resources.note: The source for the penetrance figures quoted in the cards, updated as the evidence moves. Read the ranges as ranges — risk is modified by family history and polygenic background, which is part of why the 2017 prospective estimates run higher.

resources.label: NCI PDQ — Genetics of colorectal cancer (health professional version)
resources.note: The rigorous treatment of Lynch syndrome: gene-specific penetrance for MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2, universal tumour screening algorithms, and the MLH1-methylation and BRAF reflex that separates sporadic from inherited MMR loss.

resources.label: NCI — Genetic testing for inherited cancer risk
resources.note: The practical framing: who should be offered testing, what a variant of uncertain significance means, and how cascade testing of relatives works. Useful before a first genetics appointment.

concepts.title: Cancer Genetics II — tumour sequencing, liquid biopsy and the CHIP trap
concepts.summary: A tumour test asks which drug might work — but the same mutation behaves differently by tissue lineage, a negative liquid biopsy proves nothing, and blood-derived clonal mutations routinely masquerade as tumour findings.

cards.h: What tumour sequencing is for — and why lineage still decides
cards.md:
**Tumour sequencing exists to choose drugs.** The established, label-backed examples:

- **EGFR** mutations (exon 19 deletion, L858R) in non-small-cell lung cancer → osimertinib.
- **ALK** rearrangements → alectinib, lorlatinib.
- **BRAF V600E** → dabrafenib plus trametinib.
- **HER2** amplification or overexpression → trastuzumab, trastuzumab deruxtecan.

Now the judgment point, and it is what separates a biomarker list from actual understanding. The *same* **BRAF V600E** allele in **colorectal** cancer responds poorly to a BRAF inhibitor given alone. Inhibiting BRAF in colorectal cells releases a feedback loop that reactivates **EGFR** signalling upstream, restoring flux through the pathway you just blocked; the effective regimen therefore adds an anti-EGFR antibody. Melanoma cells express far less EGFR and lack that escape route.

A biomarker is not a promise. The tissue lineage — the wiring around the mutated node — still decides whether blocking that node accomplishes anything.

cards.h: Tumour-agnostic approvals — when the molecule replaces the organ
cards.md:
**Tumour-agnostic approvals** invert the usual logic of oncology: the drug is approved for a *molecular feature* rather than for an organ.

- **Pembrolizumab** for **MSI-high / mismatch-repair-deficient** solid tumours (2017) was the first. The rationale is mechanistic: defective mismatch repair generates a high mutational burden, which generates neoantigens, which makes the tumour visible to a checkpoint-released immune system.
- The **NTRK fusion** inhibitors **larotrectinib** (2018) and **entrectinib** (2019) followed. Those fusions are vanishingly rare in common cancers but near-defining in a few rare ones, and response rates run around three-quarters — a striking figure for a population selected on molecule rather than organ.
- **Dabrafenib plus trametinib** gained a tumour-agnostic **BRAF V600E** indication in 2022.

Note the tension with the previous card. BRAF V600E has both a tumour-agnostic approval *and* a documented lineage-specific failure mode in colorectal cancer. Both statements are true: the approval reflects activity across many lineages, and the colorectal exception is handled by combining drugs. "Tumour-agnostic" means the organ is no longer the entry criterion — not that the organ has stopped mattering.

Note also what MSI-high is doing here. In Lynch syndrome it was a germline clue; in this setting it is a drug-selection biomarker. The same molecular finding answers different questions depending on why you went looking for it.

cards.h: Liquid biopsy — what a negative result does and does not mean
cards.md:
**Liquid biopsy / ctDNA.** Circulating tumour DNA is the tumour-derived fraction of cell-free DNA in plasma — often well under 1% of the total. FDA-approved comprehensive plasma panels have existed since 2020, and the operational rule is unambiguous:

**A negative plasma result does not rule out the mutation.**

Sensitivity depends on shedding, and shedding is low in early-stage disease, in some indolent tumours, and behind the blood–brain barrier. Specificity is generally good, so a *positive* plasma finding is usually actionable; a *negative* one is uninformative rather than reassuring. Plasma-first is a reasonable strategy when tissue is scarce, the biopsy is risky, or the patient is deteriorating and you need an answer this week — but a negative must reflex to tissue.

The second use is **molecular residual disease (MRD)**: looking for ctDNA after curative-intent surgery. Detectable post-operative ctDNA is strongly prognostic, and MRD-guided strategies have been used in trials to safely *de-escalate* adjuvant chemotherapy — sparing toxicity without worsening recurrence. Whether *escalating* treatment in response to a positive MRD result improves survival is a different question and is still being tested. Prognostic and predictive are not the same property, and this is the commonest place the two get conflated.

cards.h: Clonal haematopoiesis — the mutation that was never in the tumour
cards.md:
**Clonal haematopoiesis is the trap.** With age, individual blood stem cell clones acquire mutations and expand — most often in *DNMT3A*, *TET2*, *ASXL1*, *PPM1D* and *TP53*. Prevalence exceeds 10% in people past 70. This state is called **CHIP** (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential), and by itself it is not leukaemia.

Here is why it matters for a liquid biopsy. Those expanded white-cell clones shed DNA into the very plasma you are sequencing. A CHIP mutation therefore arrives in the assay looking exactly like a tumour mutation — same gene, same read pileup, plausible allele fraction. It is a documented cause of spurious *TP53* and *ATM* calls, and of patients being considered for targeted therapy on the strength of a mutation their cancer never had.

The fix is mechanical rather than clever: **sequence matched white blood cells in parallel** and subtract anything present in both. A plasma-only assay without a matched normal cannot make this distinction, and its low-allele-fraction calls should be read in that light.

Three features raise suspicion before any confirmatory test comes back: the patient is older, the variant allele fraction is low and inconsistent with the estimated tumour fraction, and the gene is one of the recurrent CHIP genes — *PPM1D* and *TP53* especially. CHIP is also independently associated with cardiovascular risk and with later myeloid neoplasm, so an incidental finding is not always nothing. It is simply not evidence about the solid tumour in front of you.

questions.prompt: A colorectal tumour carries BRAF V600E. Why does a BRAF inhibitor alone underperform here, when it works well in BRAF V600E melanoma?
options: Blocking BRAF in colorectal cells releases feedback that reactivates EGFR signalling, so an anti-EGFR agent must be combined
The V600E allele is a different mutation in colon tissue
Colorectal tumours do not express BRAF protein
BRAF inhibitors cannot reach the colon at therapeutic concentrations
feedback: Correct — this is the classic demonstration that lineage context modifies a biomarker. Melanoma cells express far less EGFR and lack that escape route; the effective colorectal regimen pairs a BRAF inhibitor with EGFR blockade.
No — it is the identical amino acid substitution; the difference lies in the surrounding signalling network, not in the mutation.
No — BRAF is expressed and mutated; the failure is pathway reactivation through EGFR feedback.
No — the limitation is biological resistance, not drug distribution.

questions.prompt: A rare salivary gland tumour with no standard systemic option is found to carry an NTRK fusion. What does this finding support?
options: Treatment with a TRK inhibitor under a tumour-agnostic approval, with response rates historically around three-quarters
Nothing — NTRK inhibitors are approved only for lung cancer
Immediate germline testing of the patient's children
Checkpoint immunotherapy, since fusions generate neoantigens
feedback: Correct — larotrectinib (2018) and entrectinib (2019) are approved on the molecular feature rather than the organ, and NTRK fusions are near-defining in a handful of rare tumours including secretory carcinomas.
No — these are tumour-agnostic approvals precisely because the fusion predicts response across many organ sites.
No — NTRK fusions are somatic rearrangements in the tumour, not inherited variants, so there is nothing for relatives to be tested for.
No — the immunotherapy rationale applies to MSI-high/dMMR tumours through high mutational burden. A single fusion does not create that neoantigen load.

questions.prompt: A never-smoker with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma has a plasma ctDNA panel showing no EGFR mutation. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Obtain tissue for sequencing — a negative plasma result does not rule out the mutation
Conclude the tumour is EGFR wild-type and start chemotherapy
Repeat the same plasma test in two weeks
Order germline testing for EGFR
feedback: Correct — ctDNA has good specificity but imperfect sensitivity, because shedding varies with tumour burden and site. Plasma-negative must reflex to tissue, particularly in a never-smoker where the pre-test probability of a targetable driver is high.
No — this is the single most common ctDNA error in practice, and it can cost a patient an effective targeted therapy.
No — repeating a test with the same sensitivity limitation on unchanged disease does not resolve the question; change the sample type.
No — EGFR-mutant lung cancer is overwhelmingly somatic. Germline EGFR variants exist but are rare and would not be the first move here.

questions.prompt: A liquid biopsy in a 78-year-old reports a TP53 mutation at 3% variant allele frequency, while the tumour tissue panel shows no TP53 mutation. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Clonal haematopoiesis — a blood stem cell clone shedding DNA into the same plasma sample
The tumour tissue panel produced a false negative and the plasma result is correct
The patient has a germline TP53 variant (Li-Fraumeni syndrome)
Laboratory contamination from another patient's sample
feedback: Correct — CHIP mutations in TP53, DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1 and PPM1D are present in over 10% of people past 70, and white cells shed DNA into the same plasma. Sequencing matched white blood cells resolves it.
No — tissue false negatives happen, but a low-frequency TP53 call in an elderly patient with negative tissue fits the well-documented CHIP artefact far better.
No — a germline variant would appear at roughly 50% allele frequency in every sample, not at 3% in plasma alone.
No — cross-contamination is rare and would not preferentially produce exactly the recurrent CHIP genes; this pattern is a recognised biological artefact, not a handling error.

questions.prompt: Detectable ctDNA after curative-intent surgery is strongly prognostic. Why does that not automatically justify escalating adjuvant chemotherapy on a positive result?
options: Prognostic and predictive are different properties — knowing who will relapse does not establish that more chemotherapy changes their outcome
Because post-operative ctDNA results are usually false positives
Because adjuvant chemotherapy has no effect on any solid tumour
Because ctDNA cannot be measured after surgery
feedback: Correct — MRD-guided de-escalation has trial support because withholding treatment from a low-risk group is directly testable. Whether escalation helps the high-risk group is a separate hypothesis still under study.
No — post-operative ctDNA positivity is fairly specific for residual disease. The uncertainty is about what to do with it, not whether it is real.
No — adjuvant chemotherapy has established benefit in several settings; the open question is whether MRD status should redirect it.
No — post-operative ctDNA measurement is exactly what MRD assays do, and it is the basis of the de-escalation trials.
