resources.note: The clinical framing of what somatic tumour testing is for, including liquid biopsy and its limits. A good companion for a learner who wants the decision logic without the molecular detail.

resources.label: NCI — Targeted cancer therapies
resources.note: Background on how targeted agents work and why a matching mutation is necessary but not sufficient — the same point the BRAF-in-colorectal example makes.

concepts.title: CRISPR I — how the editors work, and why delivery is the hard part
concepts.summary: Cas9 makes a programmable break and lets the cell improvise; base and prime editing rewrite sequence without breaking it — and getting any of them into the right tissue, then proving what else they hit, is the real work.

cards.h: Cas9 — a programmable break, and the PAM that licenses it
cards.md:
**CRISPR** — *clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats* — is a bacterial adaptive immune system: fragments of past viral invaders stored as a genetic memory, transcribed into RNA that guides a nuclease to matching DNA. The 2012 insight was that the *Streptococcus pyogenes* Cas9 system could be reprogrammed with a synthetic **single guide RNA (sgRNA)** to cut any chosen sequence.

Three components determine where it cuts:

- **The 20-nucleotide spacer** in the sgRNA, which base-pairs with the target strand.
- **The PAM** — *protospacer adjacent motif*, `5'-NGG-3'` for SpCas9 — a short sequence that must sit immediately 3' of the target. **No PAM, no cut.**
- **Two nuclease domains** — HNH cuts the target strand, RuvC cuts the other — producing a blunt **double-strand break (DSB)** roughly three base pairs upstream of the PAM.

The PAM deserves more attention than it usually gets. Recognition happens **PAM-first**: Cas9 collides with DNA, interrogates PAM sites, and only then unwinds the adjacent duplex to test whether the guide matches. This is also how the bacterium avoids destroying its own CRISPR array, which stores the spacer sequences *without* an adjacent PAM — self-versus-non-self discrimination built into the geometry.

The practical consequence is a hard constraint on targeting. If no PAM sits at the right distance from the base you want to change, that site is not addressable by SpCas9 at all. This drove the search for Cas variants with relaxed or alternative PAM requirements, now a routine part of designing an edit.

cards.h: What the cell does with the break — NHEJ, HDR, and collateral damage
cards.md:
**Cas9 does not edit. It breaks.** What happens next is decided by the cell's own repair machinery, and steering that choice is most of the craft.

- **NHEJ** (*non-homologous end joining*) is active throughout the cell cycle and rejoins the broken ends sloppily, leaving small insertions or deletions. Land one in a coding exon and you get a frameshift and a **gene knockout**. NHEJ is efficient and reliable, which is why Cas9 nuclease is excellent at *disabling* a gene.
- **HDR** (*homology-directed repair*) copies from a supplied donor template and can install a precise sequence — but it is restricted to **S and G2 phase** and is inefficient even there. It therefore barely works in the non-dividing cells (neurons, hepatocytes, mature muscle) where most genetic disease actually lives.

That asymmetry is the whole problem. Breaking a gene is easy; fixing one is not.

The break itself is also not innocent. Work from 2018 onward documented **large deletions and complex rearrangements** at cut sites, **chromothripsis and whole-chromosome loss** following cutting, and **p53 activation** that preferentially selects for p53-deficient cells in culture — an uncomfortable selection pressure to have inside a therapeutic product. Every one of those findings motivated the break-free tools in the next card.

cards.h: Editing without breaking — base editors and prime editors
cards.md:
**Base editing** (Liu lab, 2016–2017) removes the double-strand break entirely. A catalytically impaired Cas9 fused to a deaminase chemically rewrites a base within a small window of the exposed single strand:

- **CBE** — *cytosine base editor*: C•G → T•A.
- **ABE** — *adenine base editor*: A•T → G•C, using a laboratory-evolved TadA deaminase, since no natural DNA adenine deaminase exists.

No break, no donor template, and it works in **non-dividing cells** — precisely the gap HDR could not fill. The limits are equally specific: only **transition** substitutions (never transversions), **bystander editing** of other same-letter bases inside the roughly 4–8-nucleotide activity window, and the same PAM constraint on where that window can be placed.

**Prime editing** (2019) solves what base editing cannot. A Cas9 **nickase** is fused to a **reverse transcriptase**, and the guide is replaced by a **pegRNA** carrying a primer binding site plus an RT template encoding the desired sequence. The nicked strand primes reverse transcription of that edit directly into the genome. It can make **all twelve base-to-base substitutions plus small insertions and deletions**, with no DSB and no donor template.

The price is real: lower editing efficiency and a substantially larger construct. Which lands you squarely on the actual bottleneck — getting the machine into the cell.

cards.h: Delivery is the bottleneck — and how off-targets are measured
cards.md:
**Delivery is the bottleneck, not editing.** Two regimes:

- **Ex vivo** — remove the patient's cells, edit them outside the body with ribonucleoprotein, quality-control the product, and reinfuse. Maximum control, and you can sequence what you made before dosing it. Limited to transplantable tissue (blood stem cells, T cells), and it requires conditioning chemotherapy to make room.
- **In vivo** — inject the editor and let it find the tissue. **Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)** acquire an ApoE coat in circulation and are taken up by hepatocytes via the LDL receptor. That is precisely why liver targets went first, and why extrahepatic delivery — muscle, brain, lung — remains the unsolved problem. **AAV** (adeno-associated virus) delivers durably but has a ~4.7 kb cargo ceiling that SpCas9 barely fits and prime editors do not, plus pre-existing neutralising immunity in much of the population and persistent expression that prolongs off-target exposure.

Proof of concept arrived in **2025**: an infant with a lethal urea-cycle disorder (**CPS1 deficiency**, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1) received a **bespoke, patient-specific in vivo base-editing therapy**, LNP-delivered to the liver, designed and dosed within roughly six months of diagnosis and reported in the *New England Journal of Medicine*. Follow-up is short and n = 1 — but the precedent that matters is the manufacturing and regulatory path for an *n*-of-1 edit.

**Measuring off-targets.** Computational prediction alone is insufficient. Credible programmes pair *unbiased* empirical nomination — **GUIDE-seq** in cells, **CHANGE-seq** on genomic DNA, **DISCOVER-seq** via repair-factor capture — with deep amplicon sequencing of the nominated sites in the actual clinical product. Two blind spots persist: amplicon sequencing misses **large deletions and translocations** by design, because the allele simply drops out of the amplification; and a **donor's own variants** can create an off-target site that does not exist in the reference genome.

questions.prompt: You want to correct a single pathogenic A•T base pair to G•C in hepatocytes, which are largely non-dividing. Why is a base editor preferable to Cas9 nuclease plus a homology donor?
options: HDR requires S/G2 phase and a donor template, so it barely works in non-dividing cells; a base editor needs neither and makes no double-strand break
Base editors cut DNA more precisely than Cas9
Cas9 cannot be delivered to the liver at all
HDR would introduce the wrong base at that position
feedback: Correct — cell-cycle restriction is the core limitation of HDR, and it is precisely why base editing (an adenine base editor here, A•T to G•C) became the tool of choice for post-mitotic tissue.
No — base editors do not cut at all; that is the point. Precision of cutting is not the distinction.
No — lipid nanoparticles deliver Cas9 to hepatocytes efficiently via ApoE and the LDL receptor. The liver is the easiest in-vivo target, not the hardest.
No — HDR installs whatever the donor encodes; its problem is efficiency and cell-cycle dependence, not fidelity of the template.

questions.prompt: A pathogenic variant requires a G-to-C transversion plus deletion of two adjacent bases. Which tool is capable of this, and why?
options: Prime editing — its reverse transcriptase writes an arbitrary templated sequence, covering all twelve substitutions plus small insertions and deletions
A cytosine base editor, because it edits cytosines
Cas9 nuclease with NHEJ, because indels are what NHEJ produces
An adenine base editor, since any base editor can make any change
feedback: Correct — base editors only make transitions within a narrow window; prime editing removes both restrictions by templating the edit in the pegRNA. Its costs are lower efficiency and a much bigger construct to deliver.
No — a CBE performs C•G to T•A, a transition. It cannot make a transversion, and it cannot delete bases.
No — NHEJ indels are stochastic and uncontrolled. You would get a mixture of alleles, not a specified two-base deletion.
No — an ABE performs A•T to G•C only. Base editors are restricted to transitions by their deaminase chemistry.

questions.prompt: Your target base has no NGG motif anywhere near it. What does that mean for editing with standard SpCas9?
options: The site is not addressable — PAM recognition is what licenses unwinding, so without a correctly positioned PAM there is no cut
Nothing — the PAM only affects efficiency, not whether the site can be targeted
You should lengthen the guide RNA to compensate
You should raise the Cas9 concentration until it cuts
feedback: Correct — Cas9 interrogates PAMs first and only then unwinds the adjacent duplex to test the guide. This hard constraint is why Cas variants with relaxed or alternative PAM requirements were developed.
No — the PAM is a requirement, not a modifier. It is also how the bacterium avoids cutting its own CRISPR array, which stores spacers without an adjacent PAM.
No — guide length does not substitute for the PAM; the two serve different steps in target recognition.
No — more enzyme cannot create a recognition motif that is not there, and raising the concentration mainly increases off-target activity.

questions.prompt: Why did in vivo CRISPR therapies target the liver before any other organ?
options: Lipid nanoparticles acquire an ApoE coat in circulation and are taken up by hepatocytes through the LDL receptor
The liver regenerates, so HDR works efficiently there
Hepatocytes provoke no immune response to Cas9
Liver diseases are the only monogenic diseases known
feedback: Correct — the delivery biology, not the disease biology, chose the organ. Extrahepatic targeting of muscle, brain and lung remains the unsolved problem and the main constraint on which diseases are reachable.
No — hepatocytes in an adult liver are largely quiescent, which is exactly why HDR does not work well there and base editing was needed.
No — immune responses to Cas9, including pre-existing antibodies and T cells, are a genuine concern including for liver-directed therapy.
No — monogenic disease affects every organ system. The liver went first because LNPs go there, not because the diseases are there.

questions.prompt: Why is deep amplicon sequencing of computationally predicted off-target sites, on its own, an inadequate safety assessment?
options: It misses unpredicted sites and is designed in a way that drops out large deletions, translocations and chromosome loss
Amplicon sequencing is not sensitive enough to detect any off-target editing
Prediction algorithms are perfect, so the sequencing adds nothing
Off-target effects only occur with base editors, not with Cas9
feedback: Correct — you need unbiased empirical nomination (GUIDE-seq, CHANGE-seq, DISCOVER-seq) plus assays that can see large structural events, and you must consider donor-specific variants that create off-target sites absent from the reference genome.
No — amplicon sequencing is highly sensitive for small indels at the sites it interrogates. The problem is which sites and which event types it can see at all.
No — in-silico prediction is a useful filter but demonstrably incomplete; empirically discovered off-targets frequently fall outside the predicted set.
No — Cas9 nuclease has the broader off-target problem, including the structural events base editors largely avoid by not cutting.

concepts.title: CRISPR II — the approved reality and the germline line
concepts.summary: Two sickle cell therapies were approved on the same day in 2023 and only one is gene editing; what limits who benefits is cost, conditioning and access rather than editing chemistry — and the heritable-editing line sits where it does for reasons that are shifting.

cards.h: What is actually approved — Casgevy, Lyfgenia, and the difference
cards.md:
**What is actually approved.** On **8 December 2023** the FDA approved two one-time therapies for severe sickle cell disease — and only one of them is gene editing. The distinction is routinely lost in press coverage, and it matters.

- **Casgevy** (*exagamglogene autotemcel*) **is** CRISPR-Cas9. The patient's own CD34+ blood stem cells are edited **ex vivo** at the erythroid-specific enhancer of **BCL11A** — the repressor that switches off fetal haemoglobin after birth. Disabling that enhancer de-represses **HbF**, which interferes with sickle polymerisation and substitutes functionally for missing or defective beta-globin. The UK MHRA cleared it in **November 2023**, making it the first approved CRISPR medicine anywhere. The FDA added **transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia** in **January 2024**, and extended sickle cell eligibility down to **age 2 in July 2026**.
- **Lyfgenia** (*lovotibeglogene autotemcel*) is **not** editing. It is **lentiviral gene addition**: a modified beta-globin gene (HbA-T87Q) inserted semi-randomly into the genome. It carries a boxed warning for haematologic malignancy.

Notice the design choice in Casgevy. It does not correct the sickle mutation. It knocks out a repressor — an easy, NHEJ-style disabling edit of exactly the kind Cas9 does well — to reawaken a developmental programme the patient already has. That is a far more tractable engineering problem than precisely repairing *HBB* inside a stem cell, and it is why this indication reached approval first.

cards.h: The caveats: cost, conditioning, access
cards.md:
**The caveats are large, and they are not about the editing.**

- **Cost.** List prices sit near **$2–3 million**, before the surrounding episode of care — apheresis, conditioning, inpatient stay and monitoring are additional.
- **Conditioning.** Both products require **myeloablative busulfan conditioning** to clear marrow niches for the edited cells. That means infertility risk, prolonged cytopenia with infection and bleeding risk, weeks of inpatient care, and a procedure only specialised transplant centres can deliver. A patient must be well enough to survive the conditioning in order to receive the cure.
- **Access.** Most of the world's sickle cell disease burden is in sub-Saharan Africa, where none of that infrastructure exists. A therapy reaching hundreds of people is simultaneously a scientific triumph and a delivery failure.

Hold the honest summary. The editing chemistry works, and the results in treated patients are genuinely impressive. What limits the benefit is transplant medicine, manufacturing and money — the same constraints that limited allogeneic bone marrow transplant, which could already cure sickle cell disease in the minority of patients with a matched donor. CRISPR removed the donor-matching problem. It did not remove the conditioning, the cost, or the hospital.

Which is why **in vivo** editing of blood stem cells, if it can be made to work, would change who gets treated far more than any further improvement in editing precision.

cards.h: The germline line — 2018, 2025, and where the debate sits now
cards.md:
**The germline line.** In **November 2018**, He Jiankui announced twin girls born from embryos edited at *CCR5*, intended to confer HIV resistance. He was convicted in China in 2019.

The objections were substantive, not procedural. There was **no medical necessity** — established methods already prevent vertical HIV transmission with near-complete reliability. The embryos were **mosaic**, meaning different cells carried different edits. And the induced indels were **novel variants**, not the protective natural CCR5-Δ32 allele, so their functional consequences were simply unknown. Consent and oversight failures came on top of all that.

Everything described in this lesson so far is **somatic**: the change is confined to the treated patient's own cells and is not inherited by their children. That is the line. In **May 2025**, the American Society of Gene & Cell Therapy, the International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy and the Alliance for Regenerative Medicine jointly called for a **ten-year global moratorium** on clinical heritable human genome editing.

The debate has shifted since, because the technical objection is eroding. A **2026** preprint reported efficient base editing of pathogenic variants in human embryos with fewer chromosomal alterations than earlier nuclease work — while still showing mosaicism and off-target edits. The honest reading: "it is too dangerous" is a weaker argument every year, and it was never the strongest one. If safety keeps improving, what remains is governance, equity and enhancement — plus the awkward fact that **preimplantation genetic testing** already lets most at-risk couples select an unaffected embryo without editing anything, which leaves the genuinely unavoidable cases a very small set.

questions.prompt: Casgevy treats sickle cell disease without correcting the sickle mutation itself. What does it actually edit, and why does that work?
options: The erythroid enhancer of BCL11A — disabling the repressor de-represses fetal haemoglobin, which blocks sickle polymerisation
The HBB gene, converting the sickle allele back to the normal sequence
The bone marrow stroma, so it stops producing sickled cells
A liver gene that clears sickled red cells from circulation
feedback: Correct — it is an elegant piece of indirection: knock out a repressor with an easy NHEJ-style disabling edit and restore a fetal programme, rather than attempt the much harder precise correction of HBB in a stem cell.
No — direct HBB correction would require precise repair in haematopoietic stem cells and is not what Casgevy does; approaches of that kind are still in development.
No — the edit is performed on the patient's own CD34+ haematopoietic stem cells outside the body, not on stromal tissue.
No — the mechanism is intrinsic to the red cell lineage: raising HbF prevents polymerisation in the first place.

questions.prompt: Casgevy and Lyfgenia were approved on the same day in December 2023 for sickle cell disease. What is the key technical difference?
options: Casgevy is CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing; Lyfgenia is lentiviral gene addition of a modified beta-globin, not editing
They use the same editing platform but different guide RNAs
Casgevy is given in vivo; Lyfgenia is given ex vivo
Lyfgenia is a base editor and Casgevy is a nuclease
feedback: Correct — Lyfgenia inserts an HbA-T87Q transgene semi-randomly via lentivirus and carries a boxed warning for haematologic malignancy. Press coverage routinely conflates the two products.
No — Lyfgenia involves no guide RNA and no nuclease; it is a viral vector delivering an added gene.
No — both are ex vivo autologous stem cell products requiring apheresis and myeloablative conditioning.
No — neither is a base editor. Casgevy uses Cas9 nuclease; Lyfgenia uses a lentiviral vector.

questions.prompt: A patient with severe sickle cell disease asks why an approved one-time cure is still reaching so few people worldwide. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Cost, myeloablative conditioning and the need for specialised transplant infrastructure — not limitations of the editing itself
The editing frequently fails, so most treated patients see no benefit
Regulators have restricted it to research use only
Sickle cell disease is too rare for manufacturing to scale
feedback: Correct — the binding constraints are transplant medicine and economics. Most of the global disease burden is in sub-Saharan Africa, where apheresis, busulfan conditioning and prolonged inpatient care are unavailable.
No — editing efficiency and clinical results in treated patients have been strong. The gap is between who could benefit and who can access the procedure.
No — both products hold full FDA approval, and Casgevy's sickle cell eligibility was broadened down to age 2 in July 2026.
No — sickle cell disease is one of the commonest monogenic diseases in the world, affecting millions. Scarcity of patients is not the problem.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the scientific community's current position on heritable (germline) human genome editing?
options: Major professional societies called in May 2025 for a ten-year global moratorium on clinical use, while somatic editing proceeds under normal regulation
Germline editing is now permitted for serious monogenic disease in most jurisdictions
The approved sickle cell therapies are germline edits, so the line has already been crossed
The 2018 He Jiankui case was condemned purely because it lacked regulatory paperwork
feedback: Correct — ASGCT, ISCT and ARM issued that joint call in May 2025, aimed squarely at clinical heritable editing. Somatic therapies such as Casgevy are unaffected because their changes are not inherited.
No — clinical heritable editing is prohibited in most jurisdictions and is not permitted anywhere as routine practice.
No — Casgevy edits a patient's own blood stem cells. Those changes are somatic and are not passed to children.
No — the substantive objections were scientific and ethical: no medical necessity, mosaic embryos, and novel indels rather than the protective natural allele.

questions.prompt: A 2026 preprint reported efficient base editing of pathogenic variants in human embryos with fewer chromosomal alterations than earlier nuclease work. What does this most directly change about the germline debate?
options: It weakens the safety-based objection over time, leaving governance, equity and enhancement as the arguments that remain
It settles the debate — germline editing is now demonstrably safe
It has no bearing, because base editing cannot be used in embryos
It proves germline editing is the only option for couples at risk of a monogenic disease
feedback: Correct — the work still showed mosaicism and off-target edits, so it does not establish safety. But it erodes the argument that the technique is inherently too crude, which shifts the burden onto the ethical and governance questions that were always harder.
No — mosaicism and off-target edits persisted, and a preprint in embryos is a long way from evidence of safety across a lifetime, let alone across generations.
No — the study is precisely a demonstration of base editing in human embryos; that is why it drew both praise and alarm.
No — preimplantation genetic testing already lets most at-risk couples select an unaffected embryo, which is why the set of genuinely unavoidable cases is very small.

resources.label: FDA — first gene therapies to treat patients with sickle cell disease (December 2023)
resources.note: The primary regulatory record for both Casgevy and Lyfgenia, including the distinction between CRISPR editing and lentiviral gene addition that most press coverage blurs.

resources.label: FDA — first gene therapy for young children with sickle cell disease (2026)
resources.note: The July 2026 supplemental approval extending Casgevy down to age 2 — the clearest marker of how fast the label has moved since 2023. Check it for the current age and indication before quoting either.

resources.label: ASGCT / ISCT / ARM — international call for a 10-year moratorium on heritable human genome editing (May 2025)
resources.note: The current consensus statement on the germline line, and the reference point for the 2026 embryo base-editing debate. Note that it targets heritable editing only — somatic gene therapy is explicitly not in scope.

preface.hook: Every cell in you carries the same instruction book. What makes them different is which pages they read.
body: Inside almost every cell of your body sits the same set of instructions, written in an alphabet of just four letters, about three billion letters long. Your eye cells have it. Your skin cells have it. They all have the identical book.

So why is an eye not a toenail? Because cells read different pages. An eye cell keeps most of the book firmly shut and works from the eye chapter. The instructions for building a toenail are sitting right there in that eye cell, unread, the entire time.

The book gets copied every time a cell divides, which is constantly. Copying three billion letters by hand would produce typos, and copying by machinery does too — just very rarely. Most typos land on a page nobody was reading and nothing happens. Occasionally one lands somewhere that matters.

You got your book from your parents: roughly half from each, shuffled. That is why you resemble them without being either of them, and why a brother or sister got a different shuffle of the same two books.

Almost nothing about you traces back to one line of the book. Height, say, is nudged by hundreds of spots, each worth a fraction of an inch, plus how well you ate growing up. When someone says a gene 'for' something, be suspicious — that phrasing is nearly always doing too much work.

aha.title: The book is not a blueprint
aha.text: A blueprint shows the finished building. This is more like a recipe — instructions carried out in order, where timing and conditions change the result. Two cakes from one recipe can come out differently, and cells work the same way.

aha.title: Most of it is not genes at all
aha.text: Only a small slice of the three billion letters spells out instructions for building things. Much of the rest decides WHEN pages get read, which turns out to be just as important. It was written off as junk for decades, and that was wrong.

aha.title: Inherited is not the same as unchangeable
aha.text: You cannot swap the book you were given. But which pages get read responds to food, sleep, exercise and medicine. 'It runs in my family' describes where you started, not where you have to finish.

preface.closer: One book, read differently in every room of the house.
